Gradient flow and entropy inequalities for quantum Markov semigroups with detailed balance

Eric A. Carlen Address: Department of Mathematics
Hill Center
Rutgers University
110 Frelinghuysen Road
Piscataway
NJ 08854-8019
USA Email address: carlen@math.rutgers.edu and Jan Maas Address:  Institute of Science and Technology Austria (IST Austria)
Am Campus 1
3400
Klosterneuburg
Austria Email address: jan.maas@ist.ac.at
Abstract.

We study a class of ergodic quantum Markov semigroups on finite-dimensional unital C∗C^{*}-algebras. These semigroups have a unique stationary state σ\sigma, and we are concerned with those that satisfy a quantum detailed balance condition with respect to σ\sigma. We show that the evolution on the set of states that is given by such a quantum Markov semigroup is gradient flow for the relative entropy with respect to σ\sigma in a particular Riemannian metric on the set of states. This metric is a non-commutative analog of the 22-Wasserstein metric, and in several interesting cases we are able to show, in analogy with work of Otto on gradient flows with respect to the classical 22-Wasserstein metric, that the relative entropy is strictly and uniformly convex with respect to the Riemannian metric introduced here. As a consequence, we obtain a number of new inequalities for the decay of relative entropy for ergodic quantum Markov semigroups with detailed balance.

Keywords: quantum Markov semigroup, entropy, detailed balance, gradient flow.

Subject Classification Numbers: 46L57, 81S22, 34D05, 47C90

1. introduction

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a finite-dimensional C∗C^{*}-algebra with unit 𝟏{{\bf 1}}. We may identify 𝒜\mathcal{A} with a C∗C^{*}-subalgebra of ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), the C∗C^{*}-algebra of n×nn\times n matrices, for some nn. In finite dimension, there is no difference between weak and norm closure, and so 𝒜\mathcal{A} is also a von Neumann algebra. A Quantum Markov Semigroup (QMS) is a continuous one-parameter semigroup of linear transformations (𝒫t)t≥0({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t})_{t\geq 0} on 𝒜\mathcal{A} such that for each t≥0t\geq 0, 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is completely positive and 𝒫t​𝟏=𝟏{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}{{\bf 1}}={{\bf 1}}. Associated to any QMS 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}, is the dual semigroup 𝒫t†{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}^{\dagger}_{t} acting on 𝔖+​(𝒜){\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}), the set of faithful states of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. (When there is no ambiguity, we simply write 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}.) The QMS 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is ergodic in case 𝟏{{\bf 1}} spans the eigenspace of 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} for the eigenvalue 11. In that case, there is a unique invariant state σ\sigma. While σ\sigma need not be faithful, a natural projection operation allows us to assume, effectively without loss of generality, that σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}). Characterizations of the generators of quantum Markov semigroups on the C∗C^{*}-algebra ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) of all n×nn\times n matrices were given at the same time by Gorini, Kossakowski and Sudershan [31], and by Lindblad [46] in a more general setting (but still assuming norm continuity of the semigroup). Such semigroups are often called Lindblad semigroups.

The notion of detailed balance in the theory of classical Markov processes has several different quantum counterparts, as discussed below. One of these is singled out here, with a full discussion of how it relates to other variants and why it is physically natural. Suffice it to say here that, as we shall see, the class of ergodic QMS that satisfy the detailed balance condition includes a wide variety of examples arising in physics.

The set of faithful states 𝔖+​(𝒜){\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}) may be identified with the set of invertible density matrices σ\sigma on ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} that belong to 𝒜\mathcal{A}, as is recalled below. For ρ,σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\rho,\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}), the relative entropy of ρ\rho with respect to σ\sigma is the functional

(1.1) D(ρ∥σ)=Tr[ρ(logρ−logσ)].D(\rho\|\sigma)={\rm Tr}[\rho(\log\rho-\log\sigma)]\ .

We show in Theorem 7.6 that associated to any QMS 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} satisfying detailed balance, there is a Riemannian metric gℒg_{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} on 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} such that the flow on 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} induced by the dual semigroup 𝒫t†{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger} is gradient flow for the metric gℒg_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} of the relative entropy D(⋅∥σ)D(\cdot\|\sigma) with respect to the invariant state σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}. In several cases, we shall show that the relative entropy functional is geodesically convex for gℒg_{\mathcal{L}}, and as a consequence, we shall deduce a number of functional inequalities that are useful for studying the evolution governed by 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}. In particular, we shall deduce several sharp relative entropy dissipation inequalities. Some of these are new; see e.g. Theorem 8.5 and Theorem 8.6.

The Riemannian distance corresponding to gℒg_{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} will be seen to be a very natural analog of the 22-Wasserstein distance on the space of probability densities on ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} [73, Chapter 6]. Otto showed [55] that a large number of classical evolution equations could be viewed as gradient flow in the 22-Wasserstein metric for certain functionals, and that when the functionals were geodesically uniformly convex for this geometry, a host of useful functional inequalities were consequently valid. This is for instance the case when the functional driving the flow is classical relative entropy with respect to a Gaussian reference measure. In this case, the flow is given by the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, described by the Fokker-Planck equation with linear drift. One of the inequalities that is a consequence of the uniform geodesic convexity of the relative entropy is the sharp bound on entropy dissipation for solutions of the Fokker-Planck equation.

The present paper also greatly extends our previous paper [12] in which we obtained a gradient flow structure for the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. In particular, we prove a sharp geodesic convexity result for the von Neumann entropy in this setting, thereby solving a problem that was left open in [12]. Thus, our results can be viewed as a non-commutative extension of Otto’s investigation of classical gradient flows.

Mielke [50, 51] investigated related variational formulations for dissipative quantum systems based on Öttinger’s so-called GENERIC framework [53, 54]. However, the gradient flow structure considered in Mielke’s papers is in general different from the one introduced in the present paper, as the approach in [50, 51] gives rise to nonlinear evolution equations that are different from the linear Lindblad equations that we obtain here. Also, Junge and Zeng [39] have recently developed an approach to some non-commutative functional inequalities involving a non-commutative analog of the 11-Wasserstein metric.

We restrict our attention to the case that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a finite-dimensional C∗C^{*}-algebra because this setting already includes many examples of physical interest, and we wish to explain our methods in a way that does not encumber them with the host of technical and topological difficulties that would follow in an infinite-dimensional setting. For example, in an infinite-dimensional setting, it would matter that 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a von Neumann algebra and not only a C∗C^{*}-algebra with a unit, so that 𝒜{\mathord{\mathscr{A}}} would have a pre-dual, and then what we call 𝔖+​(𝒜){\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}) here would be the set of normal states; i.e., states that are continuous with respect to the weak-∗* topology on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and we would require that 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} be normal for each tt; i.e., continuous with respect to the weak-∗* topology on 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The innocent formula 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} would require closer scrutiny, and so forth. Many of the issues involved in extending our results to a more general infinite-dimensional setting are standard but not all of them. This will be done elsewhere. We also refer to a forthcoming paper for a treatment of more general transport metrics, general entropy functionals, and their geodesic convexity properties [13].

Here instead, we present a development of our methods that will be readily understood by people who are interested in the many physically interesting finite-dimensional examples. We shall also show that our methods may be applied in the infinite-dimensional setting to particular examples without first generalizing the whole theory. We illustrate this with the family of Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroups, which are always infinite-dimensional since all non-trivial representations of the Canonical Commutation Relations are infinite-dimensional. We use our methods to prove a new sharp relative entropy dissipation inequality for this family that had recently been conjectured in [38]; see Theorem 8.5. We also prove some other sharp inequalities of this type; e.g., Theorem 8.6.

While this introduction has, in the interest of brevity, used a considerable amount of terminology without explanation, the rest of the paper is elementary and quite self-contained. We do assume a basic familiarity with C∗C^{*}-algebras, von Neumann algebras and completely positive maps. Many readers will have this familiarity, but for background on C∗C^{*} and von Neumann algebras, we refer to Sakai [64], and for completely positive maps to Paulsen [59]. Terminology and facts that are used here without explanation can be found in these references.

We close the introduction with some preliminary definitions and by establishing some notation that will be in use throughout the paper.

1.1. Preliminary definitions and notation

𝒜\mathcal{A} will always denote a finite-dimensional C∗C^{*}-algebra with unit 𝟏{{\bf 1}}, regarded as subalgebra of some matrix algebra ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). The center of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is generated by a single self-adjoint element Z∈𝒜Z\in\mathcal{A}, and its spectral projections yield a decomposition of 𝒜\mathcal{A} into a finite direct sum of factors: Let {λ1,…,λp}\{\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{p}\} for some 1≤p≤n1\leq p\leq n be the distinct eigenvalues of ZZ, and let ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j} be the eigenspace with eigenvalue λj\lambda_{j}. Then each ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j} is invariant under 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and letting 𝒜j\mathcal{A}_{j} denote the restriction of 𝒜\mathcal{A} to ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j}, 𝒜j\mathcal{A}_{j} has a trivial center; that is, 𝒜j\mathcal{A}_{j} is a factor.

The structure of finite-dimensional factors is well-known: ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j} is unitarily equivalent to ℂℓj⊗ℂrj{\mathbb{C}}^{\ell_{j}}\otimes{\mathbb{C}}^{r_{j}}, and there is a unitary equivalence in which each A∈𝒜jA\in\mathcal{A}_{j} takes the form Iℓj⊗A^I_{\ell_{j}}\otimes\widehat{A} where A^∈ℳrj​(ℂ)\widehat{A}\in\mathcal{M}_{r_{j}}({\mathbb{C}}). That is, each factor may be identified in a natural way with a full matrix algebra. However, not all finite-dimensional C∗C^{*}-algebras arising in mathematical physics are factors. For example, a Clifford algebra with an odd number kk of generators, arising in the description of a system of kk Fermi degrees of freedom, is not a factor. This example will be discussed in detail later on.

Let τ\tau denote the normalized trace on AA given by τ⁡(A)=Tr⁡[A]/Tr⁡[𝟏]\tau(A)={\rm Tr}[A]/{\rm Tr}[{{\bf 1}}] for all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}. Then τ\tau is a faithful state on 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Let ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}} denote the Hilbert space formed by equipping 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the GNS inner product determined by τ\tau. That is, for all A,B∈𝒜A,B\in\mathcal{A},

⟨A,B⟩ℌ𝒜=τ⁡[A∗​B].\langle A,B\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}=\tau[A^{*}B]\ .

We could use this inner product to identify ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}} with the space of linear functionals on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, but to keep contact with the physics literature, we do something slightly different: We use the un-normalized trace to write the general linear functional φ\varphi on 𝒜\mathcal{A} in the form

φ⁡(B)=Tr⁡[A​B]\varphi(B)={\rm Tr}[AB]

for some A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}. It is easy to see that φ\varphi is a positive linear functional (in the sense that φ⁡(B)≥0\varphi(B)\geq 0 whenever B≥0B\geq 0) if and only if A≥0A\geq 0 in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. It follows that the set of faithful states on 𝒜\mathcal{A} may be identified with the set of strictly positive elements AA of 𝒜\mathcal{A} such that Tr⁡[A]=1{\rm Tr}[A]=1. Since A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A} is strictly positive in 𝒜\mathcal{A} if and only if it is strictly positive in ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), we may identify the set of faithful states on 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the set of invertible density matrices ρ\rho on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) that belong to the subalgebra 𝒜\mathcal{A}. In the following, we always write 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} to denote this set, whether we think of it as a set of faithful states or as a set of density matrices.

1.1 DEFINITION (Modular operator and modular group).

Let σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}. Define a linear operator Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} on ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}, or, what is the same thing, on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, by

Δσ​(A)=σ​A​σ−1\Delta_{\sigma}(A)=\sigma A\sigma^{-1}

for all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}. Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} is called the modular operator. The modular generator is the self-adjoint element h∈𝒜h\in\mathcal{A} given by

h=−log⁡σ.h=-\log\sigma\ .

The modular automorphism group αt\alpha_{t} on 𝒜\mathcal{A} is the group defined by

(1.2) αt​(A)=ei​t​h​A​e−i​t​h\alpha_{t}(A)=e^{ith}Ae^{-ith}

for t∈ℂt\in{\mathbb{C}}. Note that Δσ=αi\Delta_{\sigma}=\alpha_{i}.

The modular operator and the modular automorphism group are central to the characterization of an important class of quantum Markov semigroups.

First, Davies [21] identified a class of quantum Markov semigroups that he rigorously showed to arise from coupling a finite quantum system with internal Hamiltonian hh to an infinite fermion heat bath and then taking a weak coupling limit. The whole class of quantum Markov semigroups he found has the property that the semigroup commutes with the modular automorphism group αt\alpha_{t} given by (1.2) where hh is the internal Hamiltonian, and then σ=e−h/Tr⁡[e−h]\sigma=e^{-h}/{\rm Tr}[e^{-h}]. (Note that adding a scalar constant to hh has no effect on (1.2).) Of course an operator on ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}} commutes with the modular group if and only if it commutes with the modular operator.

Second, Alicki [5] showed that commutativity with respect to the modular operator is central to one natural extension of the notion of detailed balance from classical Markov chains to the quantum setting. Before explaining this fact, which is important for our work here, we first introduce some more terminology and notation.

A linear operator 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} on 𝒜\mathcal{A} is positivity preserving in case 𝒦​A≥0{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A\geq 0 whenever A≥0A\geq 0. A linear operator 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} on 𝒜\mathcal{A} is self-adjointness preserving in case (𝒦​A)∗=𝒦​A∗({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A^{*}, or, equivalently, in case 𝒦​A{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A is self-adjoint whenever AA is self-adjoint. Evidently, any positivity preserving operator is self-adjointness preserving. When 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} is a self-adjointness preserving semigroup, then its generator ℒ=limt→0t−1​(𝒫t−I){\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}=\lim_{t\to 0}t^{-1}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}-I) is self-adjointness preserving as well.

Tr[A∗ΔσB]=Tr[(ΔσA)∗B]andTr[A∗ΔσA]=Tr[|σ1/2Aσ−1/2|2],{\rm Tr}[A^{*}\Delta_{\sigma}B]={\rm Tr}[(\Delta_{\sigma}A)^{*}B]\quad{\rm and}\quad{\rm Tr}[A^{*}\Delta_{\sigma}A]={\rm Tr}[|\sigma^{1/2}A\sigma^{-1/2}|^{2}]\ ,

so that Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} is a positive operator on ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}. A dagger †\dagger will be used to denote the adjoint with respect to the inner product in ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}, or, what is the same, with respect to the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product. We will encounter many other inner products on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, but the GNS inner product associated to τ\tau has a special role. Because of the self-adjointness of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} there is an orthonormal basis {E1,…,Em}\{E_{1},\dots,E_{m}\} of ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}} consisting of eigenvectors of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}. 2. Detailed balance

There is a large literature on the detailed balance condition in a quantum setting, starting with the work of Agarwal [3], which initiated a number of investigations in the 1970’s including [5, 14, 42, 68]. Already in these papers, one finds several different, and non-equivalent, definitions. A number of more recent investigations [2, 25, 27, 48, 70] have added to the variety of meanings attached to this term. We therefore carefully explain the context of the definition that we use here, and why it is the most natural for our purposes.

Let Pi,jP_{i,j} be the Markov transition matrix for a Markov chain on a finite state space SS with elements {x1,…,xn}\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}. Suppose that σ\sigma is a probability density on SS that is invariant under this transition function: σj=∑i=1nσi​Pi,j\sigma_{j}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_{i}P_{i,j} for all ii. The transition matrix satisfies the detailed balance condition with respect to σ\sigma in case

(2.1) σi​Pi,j=σj​Pj,ifor​all​i,j.\sigma_{i}P_{i,j}=\sigma_{j}P_{j,i}\qquad{\rm for\ all}\ i,j\ .

Let XnX_{n} be the Markov process started from the initial distribution σ\sigma, so that the process is stationary. Let Pr{\rm Pr} be measure on the path space of the process. Then (2.1) is equivalent to

Pr⁡{Xn=i,Xn+1=j}=Pr⁡{Xn=j,Xn+1=i}for​all​i,j​and​all​n.{\rm Pr}\{X_{n}=i,X_{n+1}=j\}={\rm Pr}\{X_{n}=j,X_{n+1}=i\}\qquad{\rm for\ all}\ i,j\ {\rm and\ all}\ n\ .

In other words, (Xn,Xn+1)(X_{n},X_{n+1}) has the same joint distribution as (Xn+1,Xn)(X_{n+1},X_{n}), so that (2.1) characterizes time reversal invariance. There is another characterization of (2.1) in terms of self-adjointness: The matrix PP is self-adjoint on ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} equipped with the inner product

(2.2) ⟨f,g⟩σ=∑k=1nσk​fk¯​gk,\langle f,g\rangle_{\sigma}=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sigma_{k}\overline{f_{k}}g_{k}\ ,

if and only if (2.1) is satisfied.

There are a number of different ways one might generalize the inner product (2.2) to the quantum setting, and these give different notions of self-adjointness. Let 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} be a QMS on 𝒜\mathcal{A}. A state σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}) is invariant under 𝒫t†{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger} in case 𝒫t†​σ=σ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\sigma=\sigma for all t≥0t\geq 0, or equivalently, ℒ†​σ=0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\sigma=0. These conditions are equivalent to Tr⁡[σ​𝒫t​(A)]=Tr⁡[σ​A]{\rm Tr}[\sigma{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(A)]={\rm Tr}[\sigma A] for all t>0t>0 and all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}, or equivalently, Tr⁡[σ​ℒ​(A)]=0{\rm Tr}[\sigma{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(A)]=0 for all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}.

2.1 DEFINITION (Compatible inner product).

An inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle is compatible with σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}) in case for all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}, Tr⁡[σ​A]=⟨𝟏,A⟩{\rm Tr}[\sigma A]=\langle{{\bf 1}},A\rangle.

If a quantum Markov semigroup 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is self-adjoint with respect to an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle that is compatible with σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, then for all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A},

Tr⁡[σ​A]=⟨𝟏,A⟩=⟨𝒫t​𝟏,A⟩=⟨𝟏,𝒫t​A⟩=Tr⁡[σ​𝒫t​A],{\rm Tr}[\sigma A]=\langle{{\bf 1}},A\rangle=\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}{{\bf 1}},A\rangle=\langle{{\bf 1}},{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A\rangle={\rm Tr}[\sigma{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A]\ ,

and thus σ\sigma is invariant under 𝒫t†{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}.

2.2 DEFINITION.

Let σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} be a non-degenerate density matrix. For each s∈ℝs\in{\mathbb{R}}, and each A,B∈𝒜A,B\in\mathcal{A}, define

(2.3) ⟨A,B⟩s=Tr⁡[(σ(1−s)/2​A​σs/2)∗​(σ(1−s)/2​B​σs/2)]=Tr⁡[σs​A∗​σ1−s​B].\langle A,B\rangle_{s}={\rm Tr}[(\sigma^{(1-s)/2}A\sigma^{s/2})^{*}(\sigma^{(1-s)/2}B\sigma^{s/2})]={\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}A^{*}\sigma^{1-s}B]\ .

The value s=1/2s=1/2 is also special; ⟨⋅,⋅⟩1/2\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2} is called the KMS inner product. A number of its properties are developed in [61].

The inner products in (2.3) can be written as

(2.4) ⟨A,B⟩s=Tr⁡[A∗​Δσ1−s​B​σ].\langle A,B\rangle_{s}={\rm Tr}[A^{*}\Delta_{\sigma}^{1-s}B\sigma]\ .

More generally, given any function f:(0,∞)→(0,∞)f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty), define

(2.5) ⟨A,B⟩f=Tr⁡[A∗​f​(Δσ)​B​σ].\langle A,B\rangle_{f}={\rm Tr}[A^{*}f(\Delta_{\sigma})B\sigma]\ .

Note that ⟨⋅,⋅⟩1\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1} is the σ\sigma-GNS inner product whether 11 is interpreted as a number, as in (2.4), or as the constant function f⁡(t)=1f(t)=1, as in (2.5).

Let RAR_{A} denote right multiplication by AA, and define Ωσf=Rσ∘f⁡(Δσ)\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}=R_{\sigma}\circ f(\Delta_{\sigma}). Then another way to write (2.5) is ⟨A,B⟩f=Tr⁡[A∗​Ωσf​B]\langle A,B\rangle_{f}={\rm Tr}[A^{*}\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}B]. For all linear operators 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} on 𝒜\mathcal{A},

⟨A,𝒦​B⟩f=⟨[Ωσf]−1​𝒦†​(Ωσf​A),B⟩f.\displaystyle\langle A,{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}B\rangle_{f}=\langle[\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}]^{-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}(\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}A),B\rangle_{f}\ .

It follows immediately that 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is self-adjoint with respect to the inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩f\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f} if and only if

Ωσf∘𝒦=𝒦†∘Ωσf.\displaystyle\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}\circ{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}\circ\Omega_{\sigma}^{f}\ .
2.3 Remark.

For f⁡(t)=tsf(t)=t^{s}, the adjoint 𝒦′{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\prime} of 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} with respect to the inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩s\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s} is

𝒦′​B=σs−1​𝒦†​(σ1−s​B​σs)​σ−s.{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\prime}B=\sigma^{s-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}(\sigma^{1-s}B\sigma^{s})\sigma^{-s}\ .

For s=1/2s=1/2, this reduces to 𝒦′B=σ−1/2𝒦†(σ1/2Bσ1/2)σ−1/2{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\prime}B=\sigma^{-1/2}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}(\sigma^{1/2}B\sigma^{1/2})\sigma^{-1/2}. Since 𝒦†{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger} is positivity preserving if and only if 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is positivity preserving, it is evident that for s=1/2s=1/2, 𝒦′{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\prime} is positivity preserving if and only if 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is positivity preserving. However, for other values of ss, 𝒦′{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\prime} need not be positivity preserving when 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is. This is one feature that sets the KMS inner product apart from the inner products ⟨⋅,⋅⟩s\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s} for other values of ss.

In [70, Definition 16], detailed balance is defined in terms of self-adjointness with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩f\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f}, yielding a number of a priori different notions of detailed balance depending on the choice of ff. The example following Proposition 18 in [70] shows that different choices of ff can yield distinct classes of self-adjoint operators, and hence distinct notions of detailed balance. Specifically, it is shown in [70] that self-adjointness with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩1/2\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2} is not the same as self-adjointness with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩f\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f} where f⁡(t)=(1+t)/2f(t)=(1+t)/2, corresponding to the Bures metric, as discussed in [70]. The authors of [70] conclude: “The family of quantum detailed balance conditions is therefore much richer than the classical counterpart”.

However, it turns out that self-adjointness with respect to the GNS inner product, or indeed with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩s\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s} for any s≠1/2s\neq 1/2 implies self-adjointness with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩f\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f} for all ff. The argument leading to this conclusion, for which we have found no reference, is simple and will prove useful.

The following is a simple variant on the well-known KMS symmetry condition:

2.4 LEMMA.

For s∈ℝs\in{\mathbb{R}}, let ⟨⋅,⋅⟩s\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s} be the inner product defined in (2.3). Then for all t∈ℝt\in{\mathbb{R}} and all A,B∈𝒜A,B\in\mathcal{A},

(2.6) ⟨αi​t​(A),B⟩s=⟨A,B⟩s−t=⟨A,αi​t​(B)⟩s.\langle\alpha_{it}(A),B\rangle_{s}=\langle A,B\rangle_{s-t}=\langle A,\alpha_{it}(B)\rangle_{s}\ .

In particular, αi​t\alpha_{it} is self-adjoint with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩s\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{s}.

Proof.

Using the definitions we obtain

⟨αi​t​(A),B⟩s=Tr⁡[σs​(σt​A​σ−t)∗​σ1−s​B]=Tr⁡[σs−t​A∗​σ1−s+t​B]=⟨A,B⟩s−t=⟨A,αi​t​(B)⟩s,\displaystyle\langle\alpha_{it}(A),B\rangle_{s}={\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}(\sigma^{t}A\sigma^{-t})^{*}\sigma^{1-s}B]={\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s-t}A^{*}\sigma^{1-s+t}B]=\langle A,B\rangle_{s-t}=\langle A,\alpha_{it}(B)\rangle_{s}\ ,

which is the desired identity ∎

The following lemma is a result of Alicki [5] for s=1s=1, and the generalization to s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1], s≠1/2s\neq 1/2, can be found in [26, Propositon 8.1]. The following short proof, a simple adaptation of Alicki’s argument, is included for the reader’s convenience.

2.5 LEMMA.

Let σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} be a non-degenerate density matrix, and let s∈[0,1]s\in[0,1], s≠1/2s\neq 1/2. Then 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} commutes with αt\alpha_{t}, for all tt, real and complex.

Proof.

For any A,B∈𝒜A,B\in\mathcal{A},

⟨𝒦​αi⁡(2​s−1)​(A),B⟩s\displaystyle\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\alpha_{i(2s-1)}(A),B\rangle_{s} =\displaystyle= Tr⁡[σs​(𝒦​(σ2​s−1​A​σ1−2​s))∗​σ1−s​B]\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(\sigma^{2s-1}A\sigma^{1-2s}))^{*}\sigma^{1-s}B]

=\displaystyle= Tr⁡[σs​B​σ1−s​𝒦​(A∗)]=Tr⁡[σ1−s​(𝒦​(A))∗​σs​B]=⟨𝒦​(A),B⟩1−s\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{s}B\sigma^{1-s}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A^{*})]={\rm Tr}[\sigma^{1-s}({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A))^{*}\sigma^{s}B]=\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A),B\rangle_{1-s}

2.6 Remark.

Davies [21] has studied a class of quantum Markov semigroups that arise in a general model of an nn-level quantum system coupled to an infinite heat bath. He studied the weak-coupling limit and gave conditions under which the weak-coupling limit produces a quantum Markov semigroup. This procedure always yields a semigroup that commutes with the evolution given by (1.2) where hh is the internal Hamiltonian of the nn-level system. This is true whether or not the semigroup has a particular self-adjointness property. In view of Davies’ result, it is natural to focus on quantum Markov semigroups that commute with the modular operator associated to their invariant states.

2.7 Remark.

The condition that the generator ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} of a quantum Markov semigroup 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} commutes with Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} imposes strong restrictions on the structure of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}. Consider the case 𝒜=ℳ2​(ℂ)\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{M}_{2}({\mathbb{C}}). Let σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} have two distinct eigenvalues λ1,λ2>0\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>0. Let {η1,η2}\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\} be an orthonormal basis of ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} consisting of eigenvectors of σ\sigma: σ​ηj=λj​ηj\sigma\eta_{j}=\lambda_{j}\eta_{j} for j=1,2j=1,2. Then Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} has three distinct eigenvalues 11, λ1/λ2\lambda_{1}/\lambda_{2} and λ2/λ1\lambda_{2}/\lambda_{1}. The latter two eigenvalues have one-dimensional eigenspaces spanned by |η1⟩​⟨η2||\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}| and |η2⟩​⟨η1||\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}| respectively. If ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} commutes with Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}, then |η1⟩​⟨η2||\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}| and |η2⟩​⟨η1||\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}| must be eigenvectors of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} with eigenvalues, say, ν\nu and ν~\tilde{\nu}. Since A:=|η1⟩​⟨η2|+|η2⟩​⟨η1|A:=|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|+|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}| is self-adjoint and ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is self-adjointness preserving, it follows that ℒ​(A)=ν⁡|η1⟩​⟨η2|+ν~|η2⟩​⟨η1|{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(A)=\nu|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|+\tilde{\nu}|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}| is self-adjoint, which implies that ν~=ν\tilde{\nu}=\nu. Moreover, since both AA and ℒ​(A)=ν​A{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(A)=\nu A are self-adjoint, it follows that ν\nu is real. Thus ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} has at most 33 eigenvalues 11, μ\mu and ν\nu, and ν\nu has multiplicity 22 (or 33 in case ν=μ\nu=\mu). To summarize, it follows that

(2.7) ℒ​(|η1⟩​⟨η2|)=ν⁡|η1⟩​⟨η2|andℒ​(|η2⟩​⟨η1|)=ν⁡|η2⟩​⟨η1|with ​ν∈ℝ.\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|)=\nu|\eta_{1}\rangle\langle\eta_{2}|\quad{\rm and}\quad{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|)=\nu|\eta_{2}\rangle\langle\eta_{1}|\quad\text{with }\nu\in{\mathbb{R}}\ .

From here it is not hard to see that the value s=1/2s=1/2 is genuinely exceptional in Lemma 2.5. Suppose that ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is self-adjoint with respect to the σ\sigma-KMS inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩1/2\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2} for σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, where σ\sigma has distinct eigenvalues and {η1,η2}\{\eta_{1},\eta_{2}\} is an orthonormal basis of ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} consisting of eigenvectors of σ\sigma. It follows from the discussion above that if (2.7) is violated, ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} does not commute with Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}. There are many such operators ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} on ℳ2​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{2}({\mathbb{C}}). An explicit construction is given in Appendix B.

2.8 LEMMA.

Let σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} be a non-degenerate density matrix. Let 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} be any operator on 𝒜\mathcal{A} such that 𝒦​αt=αt​𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\alpha_{t}=\alpha_{t}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} for all tt, or equivalently, Δσ​𝒦=𝒦​Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\Delta_{\sigma}. If 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is self-adjoint with respect to the inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩f\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f} for some function f:(0,∞)→(0,∞)f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty), then the same holds for every function f:(0,∞)→(0,∞)f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty).

Proof.

Suppose that 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is self-adjoint with respect to the inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩f\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f} for some function f:(0,∞)→(0,∞)f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty). Let g:(0,∞)→(0,∞)g:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty) be arbitrary, and write h=g/fh=g/f. Since 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} commutes with Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}, it also commutes with h⁡(Δσ)h(\Delta_{\sigma}). Thus, for all A,B∈𝒜A,B\in\mathcal{A},

⟨A,𝒦​(B)⟩g\displaystyle\langle A,{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(B)\rangle_{g} =Tr⁡[σ​A∗​g​(Δσ)​𝒦​(B)]=Tr⁡[σ​A∗​f​(Δσ)​𝒦​h​(Δσ)​B]=⟨A,𝒦​h​(Δσ)​B⟩f\displaystyle={\rm Tr}[\sigma A^{*}g(\Delta_{\sigma}){\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(B)]={\rm Tr}[\sigma A^{*}f(\Delta_{\sigma}){\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}h(\Delta_{\sigma})B]=\langle A,{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}h(\Delta_{\sigma})B\rangle_{f}
=⟨𝒦​(A),h⁡(Δσ)​B⟩f=Tr⁡[σ​𝒦​(A)∗​f​(Δσ)​h​(Δσ)​B]=⟨𝒦​(A),B⟩g,\displaystyle=\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A),h(\Delta_{\sigma})B\rangle_{f}={\rm Tr}[\sigma{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A)^{*}f(\Delta_{\sigma})h(\Delta_{\sigma})B]=\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A),B\rangle_{g}\ ,

which is the desired result. ∎

We summarize some immediate consequences of the last lemmas in a theorem:

2.9 THEOREM.

Let σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} be a non-degenerate density matrix, and let 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} be any operator on 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Then:

(1) If 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is self-adjoint with respect to the GNS inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩1\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1}, and 𝒦​A∗=(𝒦​A)∗{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A^{*}=({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A)^{*} for all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}, then 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} commutes with the modular automorphism group of σ\sigma and moreover, 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is self-adjoint with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩f\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f} for all f:(0,∞)→(0,∞)f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty).

(2) If 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} commutes with the modular automorphism group of σ\sigma, and if 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is self-adjoint with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩f\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{f} for some f:(0,∞)→(0,∞)f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty), then 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is self-adjoint with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩g\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{g} for all g:(0,∞)→(0,∞)g:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty).

This brings us to the definition of detailed balance, which is one the various definitions that may be found in the physical literature.

2.10 DEFINITION (Detailed balance).

A QMS 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} on 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfies the detailed balance condition with respect to σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}) in case for each t>0t>0, 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is self-adjoint in the σ\sigma-GNS inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩1\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1}. In this case σ\sigma is invariant under 𝒫t†{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}, and we say that the QMS 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC.

2.11 Remark.

Every QMS 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} is self-adjointness preserving: 𝒫t​A∗=(𝒫t​A)∗{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A^{*}=({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A)^{*}. Thus, when 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC, it follows from Theorem 2.9 that

(2.8) αt′​(𝒫t​(A))=𝒫t​(αt′​(A))\alpha_{t^{\prime}}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(A))={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(\alpha_{t^{\prime}}(A))

for all t,t′t,t^{\prime} and all A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A}. This crucial observation is due to Alicki [5], and it means that 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} commutes with the time-translation governed by the Hamiltonian hh corresponding to the state σ\sigma. The condition (2.8) may therefore be viewed as a quantum analog of time-translation invariance or stationarity.

Theorem 2.9 asserts that in the presence of detailed balance, 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is self-adjoint with respect to a wide variety of inner products and also that 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} commutes with the modular group. Moreover, under the condition that 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} commutes with the modular group, self-adjointness with respect to any member of this wide family of inner products implies self-adjointness with respect to all of them. This is important in what follows.

The inner products defined just above include a number of inner products that arise naturally in the theory of operator algebras and mathematical physics. One that will be especially useful here is the Bogoliubov-Kubo-Mori inner product:

⟨A,B⟩BKM=∫01Tr⁡[σ1−s​A∗​σs​B]​𝑑s=∫01Tr⁡[σ​A∗​Δσs​B]​𝑑s=⟨A,B⟩f0,\langle A,B\rangle_{{\rm BKM}}=\int_{0}^{1}{\rm Tr}[\sigma^{1-s}A^{*}\sigma^{s}B]{\rm d}s=\int_{0}^{1}{\rm Tr}[\sigma A^{*}\Delta_{\sigma}^{s}B]{\rm d}s=\langle A,B\rangle_{f_{0}}\ ,

where

f0​(t)=∫01ts​𝑑s=t−1log⁡t.f_{0}(t)=\int_{0}^{1}t^{s}{\rm d}s=\frac{t-1}{\log t}\ .

The BKM inner product arises naturally in statistical mechanics and our work here as follows: For a self-adjoint operator hh on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H}, and β>0\beta>0, define the Gibbs state σβ\sigma_{\beta} by

σβ=1Tr⁡[e−β​h]​e−β​h.\sigma_{\beta}=\frac{1}{{\rm Tr}[e^{-\beta h}]}e^{-\beta h}\ .

The free energy is the functional ℱ⁡(β,h)=β−1​log⁡(Tr⁡[e−β​h])\mathcal{F}(\beta,h)=\beta^{-1}\log({\rm Tr}[e^{-\beta h}]). A simple calculation using Duhamel’s formula shows that for any self-adjoint AA,

d2d​s2​ℱ​(β,h+s​A)|s=0=β⁡[⟨A,A⟩BKM−(Tr⁡[σβ​A])2].\frac{{\rm d}^{2}}{{\rm d}s^{2}}\mathcal{F}(\beta,h+sA)\bigg|_{s=0}=\beta\left[\langle A,A\rangle_{{\rm BKM}}-({\rm Tr}[\sigma_{\beta}A])^{2}\right]\ .

In particular, up to a factor of β\beta, ⟨A,A⟩BKM\langle A,A\rangle_{{\rm BKM}} arises as the restriction of the Hessian of ℱ\mathcal{F} to the space of self-adjoint matrices AA satisfying Tr⁡[σβ​A]=0{\rm Tr}[\sigma_{\beta}A]=0. It is well known that for fixed β\beta, the function h↦ℱ⁡(β,h)h\mapsto\mathcal{F}(\beta,h) is the Legendre transform of the von Neumann entropy S⁡(ρ)S(\rho) on the set of density matrices. Since the gradients and Hessians of conjugate convex functions are inverse to one another, the Hessian of the free energy is the inverse of Hessian of the entropy; a fact that explains why the BKM inner product will arise naturally in the study of gradient flows of the relative entropy.

3. Generators of quantum Markov semigroups satisfying detailed balance

Since a QMS 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} on 𝒜\mathcal{A} that satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC for some σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}) has a generator ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} that commutes with the modular operator Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}, and since Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} is positive with respect to the GNS inner product, Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} and ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} can be simultaneously diagonalized. In the case 𝒜=ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), the diagonalization of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} reduces immediately to the diagonalization of σ\sigma: Let σ=e−h\sigma=e^{-h} be a density matrix on ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}. Let {η1,…,ηn}\{\eta_{1},\dots,\eta_{n}\} be an orthonormal basis of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} consisting of eigenvectors of h=−log⁡σh=-\log\sigma: h​ηj=λj​ηjh\eta_{j}=\lambda_{j}\eta_{j}. For α=(α1,α2)∈{(i,j):1≤i,j≤n}\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2})\in\{(i,j)\ :1\leq i,j\leq n\}, define numbers ωα\omega_{\alpha} (called the Bohr frequencies) by

(3.1) ωα=λα1−λα2,\omega_{\alpha}=\lambda_{\alpha_{1}}-\lambda_{\alpha_{2}}\ ,

and rank-one operators FαF_{\alpha} given by Fα=|ηα1⟩​⟨ηα2|F_{\alpha}=|\eta_{\alpha_{1}}\rangle\langle\eta_{\alpha_{2}}| where, using a standard physics notation, for η,ξ∈ℂn\eta,\xi\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, |η⟩​⟨ξ||\eta\rangle\langle\xi| is the rank-one operator sending ζ\zeta to ⟨ξ,ζ⟩ℂn​η\langle\xi,\zeta\rangle_{{\mathbb{C}}^{n}}\eta. Evidently

(3.2) Δσ​Fα=e−ωα​FαandFα∗=Fα′whereα′=(α2,α1).\Delta_{\sigma}F_{\alpha}=e^{-\omega_{\alpha}}F_{\alpha}\qquad{\rm and}\qquad F_{\alpha}^{*}=F_{\alpha^{\prime}}\quad{\rm where}\quad\alpha^{\prime}=(\alpha_{2},\alpha_{1})\ .

Alicki [5] exploited such a construction to show that for σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} with non-degenerate spectrum (in the sense that each eigenvalue of σ\sigma is simple), the generator ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} of a quantum Markov semigroup on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) that satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC (so that ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} commutes with OPENΔσ)\Delta_{\sigma}) has the form described in (3.3) below; see [5, Theorem 3]. (Alicki actually considered the more general case that ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is normal with respect to the σ\sigma-GNS inner product. His formula reduces to (3.3) when ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is self-adjoint.) The hypothesis that σ\sigma has non-degenerate spectrum turns out to unnecessary. In the context of full matrix algebras this has been shown in [42] for the alternate canonical form given in [5, Theorem 3]. It is possible to give a simple and self-contained proof of Alicki’s Theorem in a somewhat more general setting. This is done in Appendix A; the theorem proved there is:

3.1 THEOREM.

Let 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} be a QMS on a unital C∗C^{*}-subalgebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} of ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). Suppose that 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC for σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}) and that 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} has an extension 𝒫^t\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} to a QMS on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). 3.2 Remark.

The eigenvectors of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} with eigenvalues other than 11 cannot be self-adjoint on account of (1.3). However, when σ\sigma is the normalized trace, Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} is the identity, so that each VjV_{j} is an eigenvector of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} with eigenvalue 11, thus ωj=0\omega_{j}=0. Note that the operators in {Vj}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}} need not belong to 𝒜\mathcal{A} itself. The Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup in the Clifford algebra with an odd number of generators provides an example in which they do not, as we discuss shortly.

4. Restriction to commutative subalgebras

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a unital C∗C^{*}-algebra, and let σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}). Let A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} be eigenvectors of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}: Δσ​(Aj)=λj​Aj\Delta_{\sigma}(A_{j})=\lambda_{j}A_{j}, j=1,2j=1,2. Then λ1,λ2>0\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}>0, and since the modular operator is an automorphism,

Δσ​(A1​A2)=Δσ​(A1)​Δσ​(A2)=λ1​λ2​A1​A2.\Delta_{\sigma}(A_{1}A_{2})=\Delta_{\sigma}(A_{1})\Delta_{\sigma}(A_{2})=\lambda_{1}\lambda_{2}A_{1}A_{2}\ .

That is, the product of eigenvectors of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} is again an eigenvector of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}, and moreover, the eigenspace of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} for the eigenvalue 11 is an algebra. In fact, by (1.3) it is a ∗*-algebra, and it consists exactly of those elements A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A} that commute with σ\sigma. Clearly, σ\sigma itself always belongs to 𝒜σ\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}.

4.1 DEFINITION (Modular subalgebra).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a unital C∗C^{*}-algebra, and let σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}). The σ\sigma-modular subalgebra of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, denoted 𝒜σ\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}, is the C∗C^{*}-subalgebra of 𝒜\mathcal{A} consisting of the eigenspace of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} with eigenvalue 11.

Of course if σ=𝟏\sigma={{\bf 1}}, Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} is the identity on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and then 𝒜σ=𝒜\mathcal{A}_{\sigma}=\mathcal{A}. On the other hand, suppose that 𝒜=ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) and let {η1,…,ηn}\{\eta_{1},\dots,\eta_{n}\} be an orthonormal basis of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} consisting of eigenvectors of σ\sigma with σ​ηj=e−λj​ηj\sigma\eta_{j}=e^{-\lambda_{j}}\eta_{j} for j=1,…,nj=1,\dots,n. Then for each 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n, |ηi⟩​⟨ηj||\eta_{i}\rangle\langle\eta_{j}| is an eigenvector of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} with eigenvalue eλj−λie^{\lambda_{j}-\lambda_{i}}. If the numbers {λ1,…,λm}\{\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{m}\}, which are the eigenvalues of the modular generator hh, are all distinct, then the eigenspace of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} for the eigenvalue 11 is exactly the span of the set {|ηj⟩​⟨ηj|}j=1n\{|\eta_{j}\rangle\langle\eta_{j}|\}_{j=1}^{n} [5]. In this case 𝒜σ\mathcal{A}_{\sigma} is an nn-dimensional commutative C∗C^{*}-subalgebra of 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

5. Dirichlet form representation associated to a quantum Markov generator

Let ℋ=L2​(X,ℬ,μ)\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(X,{\mathord{\mathscr{B}}},\mu) be the space of square integrable real-valued functions on some probability space (X,ℬ,μ)(X,{\mathord{\mathscr{B}}},\mu). A closed and densely defined, symmetric non-negative bilinear form ℰ\mathcal{E} on ℋ\mathcal{H} defines a non-negative unbounded operator −A-A through ℰ⁡(f,g)=−⟨f,A​g⟩ℋ\mathcal{E}(f,g)=-\langle f,Ag\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}. A special case (μ\mu is a probability measure) of a theorem of Beurling and Deny [8, 9] states that Pt=et​AP_{t}=e^{tA} is a Markov semigroup if and only if for all f∈ℋf\in\mathcal{H}, ℰ⁡(f^,f^)≤ℰ⁡(f,f)\mathcal{E}(\widehat{f},\widehat{f})\leq\mathcal{E}(f,f) where f^\widehat{f} denotes the projection of ff onto the closed convex set {g∈ℋ: 0≤g≤1a.e.}\{g\in\mathcal{H}\ :\ 0\leq g\leq 1\ {\rm a.e.}\}.

A powerful non-commutative extension of this theory has been developed starting with the early work of Gross [32, 33], and continuing with [4, 16, 17, 19, 22, 30]. We shall not need the whole theory at present, but the Dirichlet form representation of the generator of a QMS will be useful to us.

Let 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} be a QMS on 𝒜\mathcal{A} that satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC for some σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}). The generator ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} can then be written in the canonical form specified in (3.4) of Theorem 3.1. Throughout the rest of this section we fix such a generator ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}, and the sets {Vj}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}} and {ωj}\{\omega_{j}\} that specify ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} in the form (3.4).

Define operators ∂j\partial_{j} on 𝒜\mathcal{A} by

∂jA=[Vj,A]so​that∂j†A=[Vj∗,A].\partial_{j}A=[V_{j},A]\quad{\rm so\ that}\quad\partial_{j}^{\dagger}A=[V_{j}^{*},A]\ .

The operators ∂j\partial_{j} are derivations, and we may consider them as non-commutative analogs of partial derivatives associated to ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}. With respect to the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product, we may then form non-commutative analogs of the gradient, divergence and Laplacian associated to ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}. We begin with the Laplacian:

Given the set {Vj}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}, we define an operator ℒ0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0} on ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}} by

ℒ0A=−∑j∈𝒥∂j†∂jA=−∑j∈𝒥[Vj∗,[Vj,A]].{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}A=-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\partial_{j}A=-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}[V_{j}^{*},[V_{j},A]]\ .

Evidently ℒ0†=ℒ0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}^{\dagger}={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}, and we may write ℒ0​A=∑j∈𝒥(Vj∗​[A,Vj]+[Vj,A]​Vj∗){\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}A=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}(V_{j}^{*}[A,V_{j}]+[V_{j},A]V_{j}^{*})}. Thus, by Theorem 3.1, ℒ0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0} is the generator of a quantum Markov semigroup 𝒫0,t=et​ℒ0{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{0,t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}} satisfying detailed balance with respect to τ\tau. We call this semigroup the heat semigroup associated to 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}, and the operator ℒ0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0} the Laplace operator associated to ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}.

We define the Hilbert space ℌ𝒜,𝒥{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} by

ℌ𝒜,𝒥=⨁j∈𝒥ℌ𝒜(j),{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}=\bigoplus_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{(j)}\ ,

where each ℌ𝒜(j){\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{(j)} is a copy of ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}. For 𝐀∈ℌ𝒜,𝒥{\bf A}\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} and j∈𝒥j\in{\mathcal{J}}, let AjA_{j} denote the component of 𝐀{\bf A} in ℌ𝒜(j){\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{(j)}. Thus, picking some linear ordering of 𝒥{\mathcal{J}}, we can write

𝐀=(A1,…,A|𝒥|).{\bf A}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|})\ .

We equip ℌ𝒜,𝒥{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} with the usual inner product ⟨𝐀,𝐁⟩ℌ𝒜,𝒥=∑j∈𝒥⟨Aj,Bj⟩ℌ𝒜{\langle{\bf A},{\bf B}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle A_{j},B_{j}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}}.

Define an operator ∇:ℌ𝒜→ℌ𝒜,𝒥\nabla:{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} by

∇A=(∂1,…,∂|𝒥|A).\nabla A=(\partial_{1},\dots,\partial_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}A)\ .

Thinking of elements of 𝒜\mathcal{A} as non-commutative analogs of functions on a manifold, we may think of 𝐀=(A1,…,A|𝒥|){\bf A}=(A_{1},\dots,A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}) as a vector field. This point of view will be justified in the next section. We define the operator div:ℌ𝒜,𝒥→ℌ𝒜\dive:{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}} by

div𝐀=−∑j∈𝒥∂j†Aj=∑j∈𝒥[Aj,Vj∗].\dive{\bf A}=-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}A_{j}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}[A_{j},V_{j}^{*}]\ .

Note that div\dive is minus the adjoint of the map ∇:ℌ𝒜→ℌ𝒜,𝒥\nabla:{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}, so that ℒ0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0} is negative semi-definite. With these definitions, ℒ0=div∘∇{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}=\dive\circ\nabla. We call ∇\nabla the non-commutative gradient associated to ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}, and div\dive the non-commutative divergence associated to ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}.

5.1 Remark.

In this finite-dimensional setting, by elementary linear algebra,

(5.1) (Null⁡(div))⟂=Ran⁡(∇).\big({\rm Null}(\dive)\big)^{\perp}={\rm Ran}(\nabla)\ .

In the terminology introduced above, elements of Null⁡(div){\rm Null}(\dive) are divergence free vector fields. Then (5.1) says that a vector field 𝐀{\bf A} is a gradient if and only if it is orthogonal in ℌ𝒜,𝒥{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} to every divergence free vector field.

The differential structure introduced above allows us to write the generator ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} of a QMS in terms of a non-commutative Dirichlet form.

As a simple consequence of the Dirichlet form representation, we state an ergodicity result. Recall that a QMS 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} is ergodic in case for each t>0t>0, the 11-eigenspace of 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is spanned by the identity, or, what is the same thing, the 00-eigenspace of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is spanned by the identity. We refer to [29] for an early study of ergodicity for quantum dynamical semigroups.

5.3 THEOREM.

Let 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} be QMS on 𝒜\mathcal{A} that satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC for σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}). Let ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} be given in the form (3.4). Then the commutant of {Vj}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}} equals the null space of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}. In particular, 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is ergodic if and only if the commutant of {Vj}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}} is spanned by the identity.

Proof.

Suppose that AA belongs to the commutant of {Vj}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}. By definition, this means that ∂jA=0\partial_{j}A=0 for all j∈𝒥j\in{\mathcal{J}}, and therefore A∈Null⁡(ℒ)A\in{\rm Null}({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}) by (3.3).

Conversely, if ℒ​A=0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A=0, then by (5.3),

0=−⟨A,ℒ​A⟩1/2=∑j∈𝒥⟨∂jA,∂jA⟩1/2,0=-\langle{A,{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A}\rangle_{1/2}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle{\partial_{j}A,\partial_{j}A}\rangle_{1/2}\ ,

which is the case if and only if [Vj,A]=0[V_{j},A]=0 for all jj. This means that AA belongs to the commutant of {Vj}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}. ∎

5.4 THEOREM.

Let 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} be an ergodic QMS on 𝒜\mathcal{A} that satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC for σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}), and let ℒ0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0} be the associated Laplacian. Then for given B∈ℌ𝒜B\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}, the equation

ℒ0​X=B{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}X=B

has a solution if and only if τ⁡[B]=0\tau[B]=0. Consequently, when τ⁡[B]=0\tau[B]=0, there is a non-trivial affine subspace of ℌ𝒜,𝒥{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} consisting of elements 𝐀{\bf A} for which div⁡𝐀=B\dive{\bf A}=B.

Proof.

Since ⟨A,ℒ0​A⟩ℌ𝒜=−⟨∇A,∇A⟩ℌ𝒜,𝒥\langle A,{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}A\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}=-\langle\nabla A,\nabla A\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}}, we have Null⁡(ℒ0)=Null⁡(∇){\rm Null}({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0})={\rm Null}(\nabla). Since 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is ergodic, it follows from Theorem 5.3 that Null⁡(∇){\rm Null}(\nabla) is spanned by 𝟏{{\bf 1}}. Since ℒ0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0} is self-adjoint on ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}, the assertion now follows from the Fredholm alternative. ∎

It is now a simple matter to write the quantum heat flow equation ∂ρ/∂t=ℒ0†​ρ\partial\rho/\partial t={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}^{\dagger}\rho in a form that leads directly to its interpretation as gradient flow for the relative entropy with respect to the normalized trace: For all ρ∈𝔖+\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+},

ℒ0†ρ=div([ρ]0∇logρ),{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{0}^{\dagger}\rho=\dive([\rho]_{0}\nabla\log\rho)\ ,

where [ρ]0[\rho]_{0} is applied to each component of ∇log⁡ρ\nabla\log\rho. As we show in the next section, it follows easily from this formula that there is a Riemannian metric on 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, which is a natural analog of the 22-Wasserstein metric, such that the quantum heat flow on 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} associated to {Vj}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}} is a gradient flow for the relative entropy of ρ\rho with respect to the normalized trace τ\tau. For a comprehensive treatment of the theory of gradient flows with respect to the 22-Wasserstein metric, see [6] and [73, Chapters 23-25].

In fact, the next lemma provides the means to extend this result to the general class of quantum Markov semigroups that satisfy detailed balance with respect to some non-degenerate state σ\sigma.

5.9 LEMMA.

Let 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} be QMS on 𝒜\mathcal{A} that satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC for σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}). and let ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} be given in the form (3.4). Then for all ρ∈𝔖+\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, and all j∈𝒥j\in{\mathcal{J}},

∂j(logρ−logσ)=Vjlog(e−ωj/2ρ)−log(eωj/2ρ)Vj.\partial_{j}(\log\rho-\log\sigma)=V_{j}\log(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}\rho)-\log(e^{\omega_{j}/2}\rho)V_{j}\ .
Proof.

By (3.5) we have Δσs​Vj=e−s​ωj​Vj\Delta_{\sigma}^{s}V_{j}=e^{-s\omega_{j}}V_{j}, and thus [Vj,logσ]=−∂s|s=0ΔσsVj=ωjVj[V_{j},\log\sigma]=-\partial_{s}|_{s=0}\Delta_{\sigma}^{s}V_{j}=\omega_{j}V_{j}. It follows that

∂j(logρ−logσ)=[Vj,logρ]−ωjVj=Vjlog(e−ωj/2ρ)−log(eωj/2ρ)Vj,\displaystyle\partial_{j}(\log\rho-\log\sigma)=[V_{j},\log\rho]-\omega_{j}V_{j}=V_{j}\log(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}\rho)-\log(e^{\omega_{j}/2}\rho)V_{j}\ ,

which is the desired identity. ∎

5.10 THEOREM.

Let 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} be QMS on 𝒜\mathcal{A} that satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC for σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}), and let ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} be given in the form (3.4). Then, for all ρ∈𝔖+\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+},

−ℒ†​ρ=∑j∈𝒥∂j†([ρ]ωj​∂j(log⁡ρ−log⁡σ)).-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\Big([\rho]_{\omega_{j}}\partial_{j}(\log\rho-\log\sigma)\Big)\ .
Proof.

Using Lemma 5.9 and (5.6) we obtain

∑j∈𝒥∂j†([ρ]ωj​∂j(log⁡ρ−log⁡σ))\displaystyle\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\Big([\rho]_{\omega_{j}}\partial_{j}(\log\rho-\log\sigma)\Big) =∑j∈𝒥∂j†([ρ]ωj(Vjlog(e−ωj/2ρ)−log(eωj/2ρ)Vj))\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\Big([\rho]_{\omega_{j}}\Big(V_{j}\log(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}\rho)-\log(e^{\omega_{j}/2}\rho)V_{j}\Big)\Big)
=∑j∈𝒥∂j†(e−ωj/2Vjρ−eωj/2ρVj)\displaystyle=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\Big(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}V_{j}\rho-e^{\omega_{j}/2}\rho V_{j}\Big)
=−∑j∈𝒥(e−ωj/2[Vjρ,Vj∗]+eωj/2[Vj∗,ρVj])=−ℒ†ρ,\displaystyle=-\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\Big(e^{-\omega_{j}/2}[V_{j}\rho,V_{j}^{*}]+e^{\omega_{j}/2}[V_{j}^{*},\rho V_{j}]\Big)=-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho\ ,

where the final identity follows from (3.7). ∎

6. Examples

6.1. The infinite-temperature Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup

As Segal emphasized [66], the Fermion number operator for nn degrees of freedom can be represented in terms of the generators of a Clifford algebra. This permits the semigroup it generates to be realized as a QMS, a fact that was effectively exploited by Gross [32, 33] using Segal’s non-commutative integration theory [65, 67].

Let {Q1,…,Qn}\{Q_{1},\ldots,Q_{n}\} be self-adjoint operators on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space satisfying the canonical anti-commutation relations (CAR):

Qj​Qk+Qk​Qj=2​δj​k​𝟏.\displaystyle Q_{j}Q_{k}+Q_{k}Q_{j}=2\delta_{jk}{{\bf 1}}\;.

The Clifford algebra ℭn\mathfrak{C}^{n} is the 2n2^{n}-dimensional algebra generated by {Qj}j=1n\{Q_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n}. Let Γ:ℭn→ℭn\Gamma:\mathfrak{C}^{n}\to\mathfrak{C}^{n} be the principle automorphism on ℭn\mathfrak{C}^{n}, i.e., the unique algebra isomorphism satisfying Γ⁡(Qj)=−Qj\Gamma(Q_{j})=-Q_{j} for all jj. The product of all of the generators Q1Q2⋯QnQ_{1}Q_{2}\cdots Q_{n} (in some order) is evidently unitary, and the CAR imply that it commutes with each QjQ_{j} if nn is odd, and anti-commutes with each QjQ_{j} if nn is even. Hence when nn is odd, the center of ℭn\mathfrak{C}^{n} is non-trivial and ℭn\mathfrak{C}^{n} is not a factor.

In the even case n=2​mn=2m, form the mm self-adjoint unitary operators i​Q2​j−1​Q2​jiQ_{2j-1}Q_{2j}, j=1,…​nj=1,\dots n. These all commute with one another, and we define

W=imQ1Q2⋯Q2​m.W=i^{m}Q_{1}Q_{2}\cdots Q_{2m}\ .

Evidently W∈ℭnW\in\mathfrak{C}^{n} is unitary and self-adjoint, and since WW anti-commutes with each QjQ_{j}, the principle automorphism is inner and is given by

(6.1) Γ⁡(A)=W​A​W=W∗​A​W=W​A​W∗for​all​A∈ℭn.\Gamma(A)=WAW=W^{*}AW=WAW^{*}\qquad{\rm for\ all\ }A\in\mathfrak{C}^{n}\ .

Let {0,1}n\{0,1\}^{n} be the set of fermion multi-indices, and for all 𝜶=(αj)j∈{0,1}n{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=(\alpha_{j})_{j}\in\{0,1\}^{n}, define Q𝜶=Q1α1⋯QnαnQ^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}=Q_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots Q_{n}^{\alpha_{n}} and |𝜶|=∑j=1nαj|{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}|=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_{j}. Let τ\tau be the canonical trace on ℭn\mathfrak{C}^{n}, determined by τ⁡(Q𝜶):=δ0,|𝜶|\tau(Q^{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}):=\delta_{0,|{\boldsymbol{\alpha}}|}. In a standard representation of ℭn\mathfrak{C}^{n} as an algebra of operators on (ℂ2)⊗n({\mathbb{C}}^{2})^{\otimes n} due to Brauer and Weyl, τ\tau is simply the normalized trace. See [11, 12] for references and further background.

Gross discussed this QMS as a fermionic analog of the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup; we refer to it as the infinite temperature Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. One good reason is that it is generated by the negative of the fermionic number operator. Another is that as conjectured by Gross [33] and proved in [11], it has the same optimal hypercontractivity properties as the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. We shall further develop the analogy here. (The infinite temperature part of the name will be justified in the next example.)

6.2. The finite-temperature Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the Clifford algebra ℭn\mathfrak{C}^{n} of dimension n=2​mn=2m for some m∈ℕm\in{\mathord{\mathbb{N}}}. Consider a set of generators

{Q1,…,Qm,P1,…,Pm},\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{m},P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\}\ ,

where

Qj​Qk+Qk​Qj=Pj​Pk+Pk​Pj=2​δj,k​𝟏andQj​Pk+Pk​Qj=0for​all​ 1≤j,k≤m.Q_{j}Q_{k}+Q_{k}Q_{j}=P_{j}P_{k}+P_{k}P_{j}=2\delta_{j,k}{{\bf 1}}\quad{\rm and}\quad Q_{j}P_{k}+P_{k}Q_{j}=0\quad{\rm for\ all}\ 1\leq j,k\leq m\ .

We think of 𝒜\mathcal{A} as the full set of phase space observables, the subalgebra generated by {Q1,…,Qm}\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{m}\} as the algebra of configuration space observables, and the subalgebra generated by {P1,…,Pm}\{P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\} as the algebra of momentum space observables.

6.3. The Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup

A set {Q1,…,Qm,P1,…,Pm}\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{m},P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\} of self-adjoint operators on a Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} is a representation of the Canonical Commutation Relations (CCR), in case for all 1≤j,k≤m1\leq j,k\leq m,

[Qj,Qk]=0,[Pj,Pk]=0and[Qj,Pk]=iδj,k𝟏.[Q_{j},Q_{k}]=0\ ,\quad[P_{j},P_{k}]=0\quad{\rm and}\quad[Q_{j},P_{k}]=i\delta_{j,k}{{\bf 1}}\ .

All representations of the CCR are necessarily infinite-dimensional, since otherwise we would have Tr⁡[[Qj,Pj]]=0{\rm Tr}[[Q_{j},P_{j}]]=0 which is incompatible with [Qj,Pj]=i​𝟏[Q_{j},P_{j}]=i{{\bf 1}}. The CCR algebra is the C∗C^{*}-algebra generated by the unitaries {e−t1​Q1,…,ei​tm​Qm,e−s1​P1,…,ei​sm​Pm}\{e^{-t_{1}Q_{1}},\dots,e^{it_{m}Q_{m}},e^{-s_{1}P_{1}},\dots,e^{is_{m}P_{m}}\} for all t1,…,tm,s1,…,smt_{1},\dots,t_{m},s_{1},\dots,s_{m}, or, what is the essentially the same thing, the Weyl operators. Not only is ℋ\mathcal{H} necessarily infinite-dimensional, but the operators {Q1,…,Qm,P1,…,Pm}\{Q_{1},\dots,Q_{m},P_{1},\dots,P_{m}\} are unbounded.

Therefore, the CCR algebra for mm Bose degrees of freedom lies outside the scope of the theory being developed in this paper. However, even without fully extending this theory to infinite dimensions, we shall be able to deduce new results for an important QMS on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, namely the Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.

To keep things simple in this excursion into the infinite-dimensional case, we take m=1m=1. Exactly as in the Fermi case, we form the operators

Z=12​(Q+i​P)so​thatZ∗=12​(Q−i​P).Z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(Q+iP)\quad{\rm so\ that}\quad Z^{*}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}(Q-iP)\ .

It is easy to check that

(6.16) [Z,Z∗]=𝟏.[Z,Z^{*}]={{\bf 1}}\ .

In one standard representation that we may as well fix here, ℋ=L2​(ℝ,γ⁡(x)​d​x)\mathcal{H}=L^{2}({\mathbb{R}},\gamma(x){\rm d}x) where γ(x)=(2π)−1/2e−x2/2\gamma(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^{2}/2} and Z=∂/∂xZ=\partial/\partial x. Then a simple computation shows that Z∗=x−∂/∂xZ^{*}=x-\partial/\partial x, and (6.16) is satisfied. Define the Hamiltonian hh by h=Z∗​Zh=Z^{*}Z. It is evident that for each kk, the linear space of polynomials in xx of degree at most kk is invariant under hh. Since hh is self-adjoint, this means the eigenfunctions of hh are orthogonal polynomials in ℋ\mathcal{H}, and hence are the Hermite polynomials. It is well known and easy to check that the kkth Hermite polynomial is an eigenfunction of hh with eigenvalue kk. That is, hh is the Bose number operator (for one degree of freedom). Fixing an inverse temperature β∈(0,∞)\beta\in(0,\infty), we define σβ\sigma_{\beta} as

σβ=(Tr⁡[e−β​h])−1​e−β​h.\sigma_{\beta}=\Big({\rm Tr}\big[e^{-\beta h}\big]\Big)^{-1}e^{-\beta h}\ .

Note that Tr⁡[e−β​h]{\rm Tr}\left[e^{-\beta h}\right] is finite by what we have said concerning the spectrum of hh. One readily finds that [Z,h]=Z[Z,h]=Z, which is the differential version of the identity

Δσβ​(Z)=eβ​Z.\Delta_{\sigma_{\beta}}(Z)=e^{\beta}Z\ .

It follows that ZZ and Z∗Z^{*} are eigenfunctions of the modular operator. (Note that since they are unbounded, they do not belong to the CCR algebra, and are only affiliated to its von Neumann algebra closure.)

Define V1=ZV_{1}=Z and V2=Z∗V_{2}=Z^{*}. Then {V1,V2}\{V_{1},V_{2}\} is a set of operators satisfying conditions (iii) and (iv) of Theorem 3.1 (with ω1=−β\omega_{1}=-\beta and ω2=β\omega_{2}=\beta), but not conditions (i) and (ii), since in the infinite-dimensional case, it is in general too much to ask that the VjV_{j} be trace-class. (However, since V1V_{1}, V2V_{2} and 𝟏{{\bf 1}} are eigenvectors of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} with distinct eigenvalues there is a natural sense in which they are orthogonal so that a natural analog of (i) and (ii) is valid.)

In any case, we may define

where {A,B}\{A,B\} denotes the anti-commutator A​B+B​AAB+BA. The operator ℒβ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta} is in fact the generator of an ergodic QMS, as shown in [18]. These authors construct the QMS first on the infinite-dimensional analog of ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}, which in this case strictly contains 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and then show that the resulting semigroup has the Feller property; i.e., it preserves 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

In [18], another detailed balance condition based on self-adjointness with respect to the KMS inner product is used. However, Theorem 2.9 and what we have said above about the modular operator shows that the semigroup also satisfies the σβ\sigma_{\beta}-DBC as defined here. In this sense, the example falls into our framework.

Simple computations show that for ∂1A=[Z,A]\partial_{1}A=[Z,A] and ∂2A=[Z∗,A]\partial_{2}A=[Z^{*},A],

(6.18) ∂jℒβA−ℒβ∂jA=−sinh(β/2)∂jA\partial_{j}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}A-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}\partial_{j}A=-\sinh(\beta/2)\partial_{j}A

for j=1,2j=1,2 and all AA in a dense domain of analytic vectors for ℒβ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta} that is discussed in [18]. We shall use this identity on this domain later to prove a sharp entropy dissipation inequality for this semigroup, as conjectured in [38, equation (9)]. Note that the corresponding formula for the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup involves cosh\cosh in place of sinh\sinh. This reflects the fact that in the Fermi case, taking the infinite temperature limit (β→0\beta\to 0) yields a QMS with a stationary state, while for the Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, this is not the case: the β→0\beta\to 0 limit cannot be taken in (6.3).

The modular generator hh has non-degenerate spectrum, and so the modular algebra 𝒜σβ\mathcal{A}_{\sigma_{\beta}} in this case is simply the set of all operators that commute with σβ\sigma_{\beta}, which is the same thing as the algebra generated by the spectral projections of hh. 7. Riemannian metrics and gradient flow

Let 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} be QMS on 𝒜\mathcal{A} that satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC for σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}). In this section we define a Riemannian metric on 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} that is determined by ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}, and for which, as we shall see, the flow given by the dual semigroup 𝒫t†{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}, is gradient flow for the relative entropy with respect to σ\sigma. Let ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} be given in the standard form (3.4). Throughout this section, {Vj}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}} and {ωj}j∈𝒥\{\omega_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}} are fixed, and we assume that 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is ergodic.

Let ρ⁡(t),t∈(t0,t1)\rho(t),t\in(t_{0},t_{1}), be any differentiable path in 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} regarded as a convex subset of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. For each t∈(t0,t1)t\in(t_{0},t_{1}), let ρ.​(t)∈𝒜\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(t)\in\mathcal{A} denote the derivative of ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) in tt. If ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) is any differentiable path in 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} defined on (−ϵ,ϵ)(-\epsilon,\epsilon) for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that ρ⁡(0)=ρ0\rho(0)=\rho_{0}, then Tr​[ρ.​(0)]=0{\rm Tr}[\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)]=0, so that by Theorem 5.4, there is an affine subspace of ℌ𝒜,𝒥{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} consisting of elements 𝐀{\bf A} for which

(7.1) ρ.​(0)=div⁡𝐀.\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)=\dive{\bf A}\ .

We wish to rewrite (7.1) as an analog of the classical continuity equation for the time evolution of a probability density ρ⁡(x,t)\rho(x,t) on ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}:

(7.2) ∂∂t​ρ​(x,t)+div⁡[𝐯⁡(x,t)​ρ​(x,t)]=0.\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rho(x,t)+\dive[{\bf v}(x,t)\rho(x,t)]=0\ .

In the classical case, for ρ\rho strictly positive, any expression of the form

(7.3) ∂∂t​ρ​(x,t)=div⁡[𝐚⁡(x,t)]\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rho(x,t)=\dive[{\bf a}(x,t)]

gives rise to (7.2) with 𝐯⁡(x,t)=−ρ−1​(x,t)​𝐚​(x,t){\bf v}(x,t)=-\rho^{-1}(x,t){\bf a}(x,t). Conversely, given (7.2) and defining 𝐚⁡(x,t)=−ρ⁡(x,t)​𝐯​(x,t){\bf a}(x,t)=-\rho(x,t){\bf v}(x,t), (7.3) is satisfied. In the quantum case, there are many different ways to multiply and divide by ρ∈𝔖+\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}.

Definition 5.7 gives a one-parameter family of ways to multiply A∈𝒜A\in\mathcal{A} by ρ\rho that is relevant here. In the next definition, we extend this to multiplication of vector fields 𝐀∈ℌ𝒜,𝒥{\bf A}\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} by ρ\rho.

7.1 DEFINITION.

Let ω→∈ℝ|𝒥|\vec{\omega}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}. For ρ∈𝔖+\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} we define the linear operator [ρ]ω→[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}} on ℌ𝒜,𝒥{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} by

[ρ]ω→​(A1,…,A|𝒥|)=([ρ]ω1​A1,…,[ρ]ω|𝒥|​A|𝒥|).[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}\big(A_{1},\dots,A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\big)=\big([\rho]_{\omega_{1}}A_{1},\dots,[\rho]_{\omega_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}}A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\big)\ .

Note that [ρ]ω→[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}} is invertible with

(7.4) [ρ]ω→−1​(A1,…,A|𝒥|)=([ρ]ω1−1​A1,…,[ρ]ω|𝒥|−1​A|𝒥|).[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}^{-1}\big(A_{1},\dots,A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\big)=\big([\rho]_{\omega_{1}}^{-1}A_{1},\dots,[\rho]_{\omega_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}}^{-1}A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\big)\ .

where we have used the fact that RρR_{\rho} and Δρ\Delta_{\rho} commute.

We are now ready to write (7.1) in the form of a continuity equation: Pick some ω→∈ℝ|𝒥|\vec{\omega}\in{\mathbb{R}}^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}, and define 𝐕{\bf V} by 𝐕=−[ρ]ω→−1​𝐀{\bf V}=-[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}^{-1}{\bf A}. Then evidently (7.1) becomes

(7.5) ρ.​(0)+div⁡([ρ]ω→​𝐕)=0.\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)+\dive([\rho]_{{\vec{\omega}}}{\bf V})=0\ .

The vector field 𝐀{\bf A} in (7.1) is not unique; however according to Theorem 5.4, the set of such vector fields is an affine space, and thus, in our finite-dimensional setting a closed convex set. It follows immediately that while the vector field 𝐕{\bf V} in (7.5) is not unique, the set of such vector fields is a closed affine subspace of ⊕|𝒥|𝒜\oplus^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\mathcal{A}, and consequently there is a unique element of minimal norm in ⊕|𝒥|𝒜\oplus^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\mathcal{A} for any Hilbertian norm on ⊕|𝒥|𝒜\oplus^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\mathcal{A}. We now define the class of Hilbertian norms that is relevant here:

7.2 DEFINITION.

For each ρ∈𝔖+\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, and the given generator ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}, define an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩ℒ,ρ\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}} on ⊕|𝒥|𝒜\oplus^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\mathcal{A} by

⟨𝐖,𝐕⟩ℒ,ρ=∑j∈𝒥⟨𝐖j,[ρ]ωj​𝐕j⟩ℌ𝒜.\langle{\bf W},{\bf V}\rangle_{{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle{\bf W}_{j},[\rho]_{\omega_{j}}{\bf V}_{j}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\ .

We write ‖𝐕‖ℒ,ρ\|{\bf V}\|_{{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}} for the corresponding Hilbertian norm.

This norm can be viewed as a non-commutative analog of a weighted L2L^{2}-norm for vector fields.

7.3 THEOREM.

Let ρ⁡(t)\rho(t) be a differentiable path in 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} defined on (−ϵ,ϵ)(-\epsilon,\epsilon) for some ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that ρ⁡(0)=ρ0\rho(0)=\rho_{0}. Then there is a unique vector field 𝐕∈⊕|𝒥|𝒜{\bf V}\in\oplus^{|{\mathcal{J}}|}\mathcal{A} of the form 𝐕=∇U{\bf V}=\nabla U with U∈𝒜U\in{\mathord{\mathscr{A}}}, for which the non-commutative continuity equation

(7.6) ρ.(0)=−div([ρ0]ω→𝐕)=−div([ρ0]ω→∇U)\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)=-\dive([\rho_{0}]_{\vec{\omega}}{\bf V})=-\dive([\rho_{0}]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla U)

holds. Moreover, UU can be taken to be traceless, and is then self-adjoint and uniquely determined. Furthermore, if 𝐖{\bf W} is any other vector field such that ρ.​(0)=−div⁡([ρ0]ω→​𝐖)\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)=-\dive([\rho_{0}]_{\vec{\omega}}{\bf W}), then

‖𝐕‖ℒ,ρ0<‖𝐖‖ℒ,ρ0.\|{\bf V}\|_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho_{0}}<\|{\bf W}\|_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho_{0}}\ .
Proof.

In view of the discussion above, it remains to show that the unique norm-minimizing vector field 𝐕{\bf V} is a gradient. To see this, let 𝐀{\bf A} be an arbitrary divergence-free vector field, set 𝐖:=[ρ0]ω→−1​𝐀{\bf W}:=[\rho_{0}]_{\vec{\omega}}^{-1}{\bf A}, and 𝐕ε:=𝐕+ε​𝐖{\bf V}_{\varepsilon}:={\bf V}+\varepsilon{\bf W}, so that ρ.​(0)+div⁡([ρ0]ω→​𝐕ε)=0\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)+\dive([\rho_{0}]_{\vec{\omega}}{\bf V}_{\varepsilon})=0 for all ε\varepsilon. Since ‖𝐕‖ℒ,ρ0<‖𝐕ε‖ℒ,ρ0\|{\bf V}\|_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho_{0}}<\|{\bf V}_{\varepsilon}\|_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho_{0}} for all ε\varepsilon, it follows that ⟨𝐕,𝐖⟩ℒ,ρ0=0\langle{\bf V},{\bf W}\rangle_{{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho_{0}}}=0, and therefore ⟨𝐕,𝐀⟩ℌ𝒜=0\langle{{\bf V},{\bf A}}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}=0. This means that 𝐕{\bf V} is orthogonal to the set of divergence-free vector fields, hence it is the gradient of some U∈𝒜U\in{\mathord{\mathscr{A}}}. By subtracting a multiple of the identity, we may take UU to be traceless, and then UU is uniquely determined, in view of Theorem 5.3 and the ergodicity of 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}.

(7.7) ℒρA=div([ρω→]∇A).{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho}A=\dive([\rho_{\vec{\omega}}]\nabla A)\ .

Now use the fact that {Vj}j∈𝒥={Vj∗}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}=\{V_{j}^{*}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}} and that for all j∈𝒥j\in{\mathcal{J}}, Δσ​(Vj)=e−ωj​Vj\Delta_{\sigma}(V_{j})=e^{-\omega_{j}}V_{j} and Δσ​(Vj∗)=eωj​Vj∗\Delta_{\sigma}(V_{j}^{*})=e^{\omega_{j}}V_{j}^{*}. It follows that (ℒρ​A)∗=ℒρ​A∗({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\rho}A^{*}. 7.4 DEFINITION.

For each ρ∈𝔖+\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, we identify the tangent space TρT_{\rho} at ρ=ρ0\rho=\rho_{0}, with the set of gradients vector fields 𝒢:={∇U:U∈𝒜,U=U∗}\mathcal{G}:=\{\nabla U\ :\ U\in{\mathord{\mathscr{A}}}\ ,\ U=U^{*}\} through the one-to-one correspondence provided by (7.6). ‖ρ.​(0)‖gℒ,ρ2=‖𝐕‖ℒ,ρ2\|\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0)\|^{2}_{g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}}=\|{\bf V}\|_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}^{2}\

where ρ.​(0)\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(0) and 𝐕{\bf V} are related by (7.6).

The metric we have just defined is C∞C^{\infty}. div[ρ]ω→∇X=Ak.\dive[\rho]_{\vec{\omega}}\nabla X=A_{k}\ .

[gℒ(ρ)]k,ℓ=∑j∈𝒥⟨∇Xk(ρ),[ρ]ωj∇Xℓ(ρ)⟩ℌ𝒜,[g_{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(\rho)]_{k,\ell}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle\nabla X_{k}(\rho),[\rho]_{\omega_{j}}\nabla X_{\ell}(\rho)\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\ ,

Thus, for each k,ℓk,\ell, [gℒ​(ρ)]k,ℓ[g_{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}(\rho)]_{k,\ell} is a C∞C^{\infty} function of ρ\rho.

Now let ℱ:𝔖+→ℝ{\mathcal{F}}:{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}\to{\mathbb{R}} be a differentiable function. The differential of ℱ{\mathcal{F}}, denoted δ​ℱδ​ρ​(ρ){\displaystyle\frac{\delta{\mathcal{F}}}{\delta\rho}(\rho)}, is the unique traceless self-adjoint element in 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfying

(7.8) limt→01t​(ℱ⁡(ρ+t​A)−ℱ⁡(ρ))=Tr⁡[δ​ℱδ​ρ​(ρ)​A]\displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t}\big({\mathcal{F}}(\rho+tA)-{\mathcal{F}}(\rho)\big)={\rm Tr}\left[\displaystyle\frac{\delta{\mathcal{F}}}{\delta\rho}(\rho)A\right]
