The ultimate term in (7) is, apart from a trivial factor of 44, precisely how the metric tensor was defined in [12].

This shows two things: First, that Theorem 7.6 is an extension, and not merely an analog, of our work in [12]. Second, it makes available to us the differential calculus based on the skew derivations when studying the geometry associated to the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. (We have explicitly discussed the infinite temperature case, but the same reasoning applies in general.) Since the skew derivations have the property of “lowering polynomial degree by one” for the eigenfunctions of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}, as discussed between (6.12) and (6.13), this alternate formulation of the metric will be extremely helpful in the next section.

8. Geodesic convexity and relaxation to equilibrium

In this section we develop the advantages of having written the evolution equation (7.10) as gradient flow for the relative entropy. We draw on work of Otto and Westdickenberg [57] and Daneri and Savaré [20]. Both pairs of authors were primarily interested in infinite-dimensional problems concerning metrics on spaces of probability densities, but several of their results are new and interesting in finite dimension. The approach of Otto and Westdickenberg is thoroughly developed in the finite-dimensional setting in Section 2 of [20]. We briefly summarize what we need.

Let (ℳ,g)(\mathcal{M},g) be any smooth, finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold. For x,yx,y in ℳ\mathcal{M}, the Riemannian distance dg​(x,y)d_{g}(x,y) between xx and yy is given by minimizing an action integral of paths γ:[0,1]→ℳ\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathcal{M} running from xx to yy:

dg2(x,y)=inf{∫01∥γ.(s)∥g⁡(γ⁡(s))2ds:γ(0)=x,γ(1)=y},d_{g}^{2}(x,y)=\inf\left\{\int_{0}^{1}\|\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s)\|^{2}_{g(\gamma(s))}\>{\rm d}s\ :\ \gamma(0)=x,\ \gamma(1)=y\right\}\ ,

where

‖γ.​(s)‖g⁡(γ⁡(s))2=gγ⁡(s)​(γ.​(s),γ.​(s)).\|\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s)\|^{2}_{g(\gamma(s))}=g_{\gamma(s)}(\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s),\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s))\ .

(If the infimum is achieved, any minimizer γ\gamma will be a geodesic.) If FF is a smooth function on ℳ\mathcal{M}, let gradg​F{\rm grad}_{g}F denote its Riemannian gradient. Consider the semigroup StS_{t} of transformations on ℳ\mathcal{M} given by solving γ˙​(t)=−gradg​F​(γ⁡(t))\dot{\gamma}(t)=-{\rm grad}_{g}F(\gamma(t)); we assume for now that nice global solutions exist. The semigroup StS_{t}, t≥0t\geq 0, is gradient flow for FF.

For λ∈ℝ\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}}, the function FF is λ\lambda-convex in case whenever γ:[0,1]→ℳ\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathcal{M} is a distance minimizing geodesic, then for all s∈(0,1)s\in(0,1),

d2d​s2​F​(γ⁡(s))≥λ​g​(γ.​(s),γ.​(s)).\frac{{\rm d}^{2}}{{\rm d}s^{2}}F(\gamma(s))\geq\lambda g(\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s),\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\gamma}(s))\ .

It is a standard result that whenever FF is λ\lambda-convex, the gradient flow for FF is λ\lambda-contracting in the sense that for all x,y∈ℳx,y\in\mathcal{M} and t>0t>0,

(8.1) dd​t​dg2​(St​(x),St​(y))≤−2​λ​dg2​(St​(x),St​(y)).\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}d_{g}^{2}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))\leq-2\lambda d_{g}^{2}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))\ .

Otto and Westdickenberg [57] developed an approach to geodesic convexity that takes (8.1) as its starting point. Let {γ⁡(s)}s∈[0,1]\{\gamma(s)\}_{s\in[0,1]} be any smooth path in ℳ\mathcal{M} with γ⁡(0)=x\gamma(0)=x and γ⁡(1)=y\gamma(1)=y. They use the gradient flow transformation StS_{t} to define a one-parameter family of paths γt:[0,1]→ℳ\gamma^{t}:[0,1]\to\mathcal{M}, t≥0t\geq 0 defined by

γt​(s)=St​γ​(s).\gamma^{t}(s)=S_{t}\gamma(s)\ .

Since γt\gamma^{t} is admissible for the variational problem that defines dg​(St​(x),St​(y))d_{g}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y)), it is immediate that for each t≥0t\geq 0,

(8.2) dg2​(St​(x),St​(y))≤∫01‖dd​s​γt​(s)‖g​(γt​(s))2​𝑑s.d_{g}^{2}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))\leq\int_{0}^{1}\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\gamma^{t}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\gamma^{t}(s))}\>{\rm d}s\ .

In the present smooth setting it is shown in [20, (2.8) – (2.11)] that if for all smooth curves γ:[0,1]→ℳ\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathcal{M},

(8.3) dd​t|0+​(‖dd​s​γt​(s)‖g​(γt​(s))2)≤−2​λ​‖dd​s​γ0​(s)‖g​(γ0​(s))2,\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\bigg|_{0+}\left(\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\gamma^{t}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\gamma^{t}(s))}\right)\leq-2\lambda\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\gamma^{0}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\gamma^{0}(s))}\ ,

for all s∈(0,1)s\in(0,1), then FF is geodesically λ\lambda-convex.

To see the connection between (8.3) and the contraction property, suppose that xx and yy are connected by a minimal geodesic γ\gamma so that

dg2​(x,y)=∫01‖dd​s​γ​(s)‖g⁡(γ⁡(s))2​𝑑s.d_{g}^{2}(x,y)=\int_{0}^{1}\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\gamma(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\gamma(s))}\>{\rm d}s\ .

(If xx and yy are sufficiently close, this is the case.) Then (8.2) and (8.3) combine to yield

dd​t|0+​dg2​(St​(x),St​(y))≤−2​λ​dg2​(x,y),\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\bigg|_{0+}d_{g}^{2}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))\leq-2\lambda d_{g}^{2}(x,y)\ ,

and then, provided that St​(x)S_{t}(x) and St​(y)S_{t}(y) continue to be connected by a minimal geodesic for all tt, the semigroup property of StS_{t} yields the exponential λ\lambda-contractivity of the flow:

(8.4) dg​(St​(x),St​(y))≤e−λ​t​dg​(x,y).d_{g}(S_{t}(x),S_{t}(y))\leq e^{-\lambda t}d_{g}(x,y)\ .

The local argument in [20] proves the geodesic λ\lambda-convexity of FF when (8.3) is valid for all smooth paths in ℳ\mathcal{M}, and thus leads to (8.4) without any assumptions of geodesic completeness.

When (8.3) is valid for some λ>0\lambda>0, and hence also (8.4) for the same λ\lambda, FF has at most one fixed point x0x_{0} in ℳ\mathcal{M}, which is necessarily a strict minimizer of FF on ℳ\mathcal{M}. We may normalize F⁡(x0)=0F(x_{0})=0, and then under the geodesic λ\lambda-convexity of FF, is it well known that for all xx,

(8.5) dd​t​F​(St​(x))≤−2​λ​F​(St​(x)),\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}F(S_{t}(x))\leq-2\lambda F(S_{t}(x))\ ,

which gives us another way to measure the rate of convergence to the fixed point under the flow StS_{t}.

There is also a more direct route from (8.3) to (8.5). If γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) is given by the gradient flow of FF through γ​(t)=St​(x)\gamma(t)=S_{t}(x), then

(8.6) dd​t​F​(γ⁡(t))=−‖gradg​F​(γ⁡(t))‖g⁡(γ⁡(t))2.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}F(\gamma(t))=-\|{\rm grad}_{g}F(\gamma(t))\|^{2}_{g(\gamma(t))}\ .

Define the energy function EE associated to FF by

(8.7) E⁡(x)=‖gradg​F​(x)‖g⁡(x)2.E(x)=\|{\rm grad}_{g}F(x)\|^{2}_{g(x)}\ .

Then (8.3) applied with γt​(s)=Ss+t​(x)\gamma^{t}(s)=S_{s+t}(x) together with the semigroup property yields

dd​t​E​(St​(x))≤−2​λ​E​(St​(x)).\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}E(S_{t}(x))\leq-2\lambda E(S_{t}(x))\ .

Hence (8.3) not only leads to the contractivity property (8.4), but also to the exponential convergence estimates

(8.8) F⁡(St​(x))≤e−2​λ​t​F​(x)andE⁡(St​(x))≤e−2​λ​t​E​(x).F(S_{t}(x))\leq e^{-2\lambda t}F(x)\quad{\rm and}\quad E(S_{t}(x))\leq e^{-2\lambda t}E(x)\ .

Moreover, combining (8.8) with (8.6) and (8.7), we obtain the inequality

(8.9) F⁡(x)≤12​λ​E​(x).F(x)\leq\frac{1}{2\lambda}E(x)\ .

In our setting, when FF is a relative entropy function, (8.9) will be a generalized logarithmic Sobolev inequality.

The relations between (8.4) and the bounds in (8.8) and geodesic convexity of FF have all been discussed by Otto [55] as the basis of his approach to quantitative estimates on the rates of relaxation for solutions of the porous medium equation.

Thus, to prove geodesic convexity of FF, and hence (8.4) and (8.8), it suffices to prove (8.3). This first derivative estimate can provide a much easier route to a proof of λ\lambda-convexity of FF than direct calculation of the Hessian of FF followed by an estimate of its least eigenvalue. The point of view of Otto and Westdickenberg is that this approach can be especially fruitful in an infinite-dimensional setting (such as that of [55]) given all the regularity issues to go along with computing the Hessian of FF. In the remainder of this section, we shall show that it is also quite fruitful in our finite-dimensional setting. Related work in the commutative setting can be found in [23, 24, 28, 45, 47, 49]. For the difficulties relating to direct computation and analysis of the Hessian even for the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, see our previous paper [12].

8.1. Geodesic convexity using intertwining relations

For the rest of this section, let σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, and fix 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}, an ergodic QMS that satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC. Let ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} be given in the standard form (3.4), so that the data specifying ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} are the sets {Vj}j∈𝒥\{V_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}} and {ωj}j∈𝒥\{\omega_{j}\}_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}. Let ∇:ℌ𝒜→ℌ𝒜,𝒥\nabla:{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} and div:ℌ𝒜,𝒥→ℌ𝒜\dive:{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}} be the associated non-commutative gradient and divergence (as opposed to the associated Riemannian gradient and divergence).

Let ρ:[0,1]→𝔖+\rho:[0,1]\to{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} be a smooth path in 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, and define the one-parameter family of paths, ρt​(s)\rho^{t}(s), (s,t)∈[0,1]×[0,∞)(s,t)\in[0,1]\times[0,\infty) by

ρt​(s)=𝒫t†​ρ​(s).\rho^{t}(s)={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(s)\ .

By what has been explained above, it we can prove that

(8.10) dd​t|0+​(‖dd​s​ρt​(s)‖g​(ρt​(s))2)≤−2​λ​‖dd​s​ρ0​(s)‖g​(ρ0​(s))2\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}t}\bigg|_{0+}\left(\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\rho^{t}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\rho^{t}(s))}\right)\leq-2\lambda\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\rho^{0}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\rho^{0}(s))}

for all smooth ρ:[0,1]→ℳ\rho:[0,1]\to\mathcal{M} and all s∈(0,1)s\in(0,1), we will have proved the geodesic convexity of the relative entropy functional, and consequently, we shall have proved

D(𝒫t†ρ||σ)≤e−2​λ​tD(ρ||σ).D({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho||\sigma)\leq e^{-2\lambda t}D(\rho||\sigma)\ .

We now present a simple sufficient condition for (8.10) that we shall be able to verify in a number of interesting examples.

8.1 DEFINITION.

A semigroup 𝒫→t\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} on ℌ𝒜,𝒥{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}} intertwines with a semigroup 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} on ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}} in case for all t>0t>0, and all A∈ℌ𝒜A\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}},

(8.11) ∇𝒫tA=𝒫→t∇A.\nabla{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A=\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}\nabla A\ .

By duality, the intertwining relation ∇∘𝒫t=𝒫t→∘∇\nabla\circ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=\vec{{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}}\circ\nabla implies the identity

𝒫t†​div⁡(𝐀)=div⁡(𝒫t→†​𝐀),for ​𝐀∈ℌ𝒜,𝒥.\displaystyle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\dive({\bf A})=\dive(\vec{{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}}^{\dagger}{\bf A})\;,\qquad\text{for }{\bf A}\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A},{\mathcal{J}}}\ .

We will be particularly interested in cases in which for some λ∈ℝ\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}},

(8.12) 𝒫→t​𝐀=(e−λ​t​𝒫t​A1,…,e−λ​t​𝒫t​A|𝒥|).\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}{\bf A}=(e^{-\lambda t}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A_{1},\dots,e^{-\lambda t}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|})\ .
8.2 Remark.

A classical example is provided by the Mehler formula for the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, which was first studied by Mehler in 1866. For β>0\beta>0, let γβ(x)=(β/2π)n/2e−β|x|2/2\gamma_{\beta}(x)=(\beta/2\pi)^{n/2}e^{-\beta|x|^{2}/2} be the centered Gaussian density on ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} with zero mean and variance n/βn/\beta. For t>0t>0 and bounded continuous functions ff on ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n}, define Pt​fP_{t}f by

(8.13) Pt​f​(x)=∫ℝnf⁡(e−t​x+(1−e−2​t)1/2​y)​γβ​(y)​𝑑y.P_{t}f(x)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}f(e^{-t}x+(1-e^{-2t})^{1/2}y)\gamma_{\beta}(y)\>{\rm d}y\ .

Then PtP_{t} is a classical Markov semigroup; namely the Mehler or Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. The dual semigroup Pt†P_{t}^{\dagger} acting on probability densities ρ\rho on ℝn{\mathbb{R}}^{n} is defined by

∫ℝnPt†​ρ​(x)​f​(x)​𝑑x=∫ℝnρ⁡(x)​Pt​f​(x)​𝑑x\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}P_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(x)f(x)\>{\rm d}x=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}\rho(x)P_{t}f(x)\>{\rm d}x

A change of variables yields the dual Mehler formula:

Pt†​ρ​(x)=∫ℝnρ⁡(e−t​x−(1−e−2​t)1/2​y)​γβ​((1−e−2​t)1/2​x+e−t​y)​𝑑y.P_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(x)=\int_{{\mathbb{R}}^{n}}\rho\big(e^{-t}x-(1-e^{-2t})^{1/2}y\big)\gamma_{\beta}\big((1-e^{-2t})^{1/2}x+e^{-t}y\big)\>{\rm d}y\ .

A Taylor expansion in (8.13) and then integration by parts show that f⁡(x,t):=Pt​f​(x)f(x,t):=P_{t}f(x) and ρ⁡(x,t):=Pt†​ρ​(x)\rho(x,t):=P_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(x) satisfy

∂∂tf(x,t)=(1βdiv−x)∇f(x,t)and∂∂tρ(x,t)=div(1β∇+x)ρ(x,t).\frac{\partial}{\partial t}f(x,t)=\left(\frac{1}{\beta}\dive-x\right)\nabla f(x,t)\quad{\rm and}\quad\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\rho(x,t)=\dive\left(\frac{1}{\beta}\nabla+x\right)\rho(x,t)\ .

It is immediate from (8.13) that

(8.14) ∇Ptf(x)=P→t∇f(x)\nabla P_{t}f(x)=\ \vec{P}_{t}\nabla f(x)

where P→t​(v1,…​vn)​(x)=e−t​(Pt​v1​(x),…,Pt​vn​(x))\vec{P}_{t}(v_{1},\dots v_{n})(x)=e^{-t}(P_{t}v_{1}(x),\dots,P_{t}v_{n}(x)). We shall see below that an identity similar to (8.14) is readily proved for the Fermi and Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup.

Using (8.14), which is a direct analog of (8.11) and (8.12), Ledoux [44, p. 447] gave a very simple proof of the optimal logarithmic Sobolev inequality for the classical Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup. A key element in his proof is the joint convexity of (a,r)↦|a|2/r(a,r)\mapsto|a|^{2}/r on ℝn×(0,∞){\mathbb{R}}^{n}\times(0,\infty), for which we will need a suitable non-commutative analogue.

The latter is provided by a well-known convexity inequality for matrices, which asserts that, for all ω∈ℝ\omega\in{\mathbb{R}}, the mapping

(8.15) (ρ,A)↦⟨A,[ρ]ω−1A⟩ℌ𝒜=Tr[∫0∞(t𝟏+e−ω/2ρ)−1A∗(t𝟏+eω/2ρ)−1Adt]\displaystyle(\rho,A)\mapsto\langle A,[\rho]_{{\omega}}^{-1}A\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}={\rm Tr}\bigg[\int_{0}^{\infty}(t{{\bf 1}}+e^{-\omega/2}\rho)^{-1}A^{*}(t{{\bf 1}}+e^{\omega/2}\rho)^{-1}A\>{\rm d}t\bigg]

is jointly convex on 𝔖+×𝒜{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}\times\mathcal{A}; see [36, 37]. Note that if ρ\rho and AA are scalars, the right-hand side reduces to A2/ρA^{2}/\rho. The non-commutative convexity result ultimately derives from Lieb’s concavity Theorem [41]. Since 𝒫t†{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger} is completely positive, it follows from (8.15) that

(8.16) ⟨𝒫t†​A,[𝒫t†​ρ]ω−1​𝒫t†​A⟩ℌ𝒜≤⟨A,[ρ]ω−1​A⟩ℌ𝒜.\displaystyle\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A,[{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho]_{{\omega}}^{-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\leq\langle A,[\rho]_{{\omega}}^{-1}A\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\ .

There is a well-developed theory of monotone metrics beginning with work of Chentsov and Morozova [52] for classical Markov processes and its non-commutative extension initiated by Petz [62], and further developed in [40, 34, 60, 35, 70]. Other results from this theory will be useful in further developments.

Now consider any smooth path ρ:[0,1]→𝔖+\rho:[0,1]\to{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, and for each s∈(0,1)s\in(0,1) write

ρ.​(s)=div⁡𝐀​(s)\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(s)=\dive{\bf A}(s)

where 𝐀⁡(s){\bf A}(s) is the solution of ρ.​(s)=div⁡𝐀​(s)\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(s)=\dive{\bf A}(s) that minimizes ⟨𝐀,[ρ]ω→−1​𝐀⟩ℒ,ρ\langle{\bf A},[\rho]_{{\vec{\omega}}}^{-1}{\bf A}\rangle_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho} so that, by the definitions in Section 7,

gℒ,ρ​(ρ.​(s),ρ.​(s))=∑j∈𝒥⟨Aj​(s),[ρ⁡(s)]ωj−1​Aj​(s)⟩ℌ𝒜.g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho}(\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(s),\accentset{\mbox{\large.}}{\rho}(s))=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle A_{j}(s),[\rho(s)]_{{\omega_{j}}}^{-1}A_{j}(s)\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\ .

Set ρt​(s):=𝒫t†​ρ​(s)\rho^{t}(s):={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(s), and suppose that the semigroup 𝒫→t\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} defined by (8.12) intertwines with 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}. It follows that

dd​s​ρt​(s)=𝒫t†​div⁡𝐀⁡(s)=div⁡𝒫→t†​𝐀​(s).\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\rho^{t}(s)={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\dive{\bf A}(s)=\dive\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}{\bf A}(s)\ .

Consequently, by (8.12) and (8.16),

‖dd​s​ρt​(s)‖g​(ρt​(s))2\displaystyle\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\rho^{t}(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\rho^{t}(s))} ≤\displaystyle\leq e−2​λ​t​∑j∈𝒥⟨𝒫t†​Aj​(s),[𝒫t†​ρ​(s)]ωj−1​𝒫t†​Aj​(s)⟩ℌ𝒜\displaystyle e^{-2\lambda t}\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{j}(s),[{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho(s)]_{{\omega_{j}}}^{-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{j}(s)\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}
≤\displaystyle\leq e−2​λ​t​∑j∈𝒥⟨Aj​(s),[ρ⁡(s)]ωj−1​Aj​(s)⟩ℌ𝒜=e−2​λ​t​‖dd​s​ρ​(s)‖g⁡(ρ⁡(s))2,\displaystyle e^{-2\lambda t}\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle A_{j}(s),[\rho(s)]_{{\omega_{j}}}^{-1}A_{j}(s)\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}=e^{-2\lambda t}\left\|\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm d}s}\rho(s)\right\|^{2}_{g(\rho(s))}\ ,

which clearly implies (8.10). Altogether we have proved:

8.3 THEOREM.

Let σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, and let 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}} be an ergodic QMS that satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC. Let ∇\nabla and div\dive denote the associated non-commutative gradient and divergence. Suppose that for some λ>0\lambda>0, the semigroup 𝒫→t\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} defined by (8.12) intertwines with 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}. Then the relative entropy with respect to σ\sigma is geodesically λ\lambda-convex on 𝔖+{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} for the Riemannian metric (gℒ,ρ)ρ(g_{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}},\rho})_{\rho}. Moreover, the exponential convergence estimate

D(𝒫t†ρ||σ)≤e−2​λ​tD(ρ||σ)\displaystyle D({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho||\sigma)\leq e^{-2\lambda t}D(\rho||\sigma)

holds, as well as the generalized logarithmic Sobolev inequality

(8.17) D(ρ||σ)≤12​λτ[−ℒ†(ρ)(logρ−logσ)].\displaystyle D(\rho||\sigma)\leq\frac{1}{2\lambda}\tau\big[-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}(\rho)\big(\log\rho-\log\sigma\big)\big]\ .

While it is a problem of ongoing research to extend Theorem 8.3 to the infinite dimensional setting, the part of it concerning entropy and entropy production inequalities is relatively robust, as it relies most essentially on Lieb’s convexity result, while the part of it concerning geodesic convexity is more involved and requires more work to generalize. Therefore, with regard to the infinite dimensional Bose-Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup, we are not presently in a positions to make any statements about geodesic convexity of the entropy, but the situation is much better concerning entropy and entropy production.

Let 𝒟⁡[ρ]=τ⁡[−ℒ†​(ρ)​(log⁡ρ−log⁡σ)]\mathcal{D}[\rho]=\tau\big[-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}(\rho)\big(\log\rho-\log\sigma\big)\big] be the entropy dissipation functional, which is minus the derivative of D(𝒫t†ρ||σ)D({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho||\sigma) at t=0t=0. By Theorem 5.10,

−ℒ†​ρ=∑j∈𝒥∂j†([ρ]ωj​∂j(log⁡ρ−log⁡σ))=div⁡(𝐀).-{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\partial_{j}^{\dagger}\Big([\rho]_{\omega_{j}}\partial_{j}(\log\rho-\log\sigma)\Big)={\rm div}({\bf A})\ .

The entropy dissipation functional 𝒟⁡[ρ]\mathcal{D}[\rho] is then given by

𝒟⁡[ρ]=∑j∈𝒥⟨Aj,[ρ]ωj−1​Aj⟩ℌ𝒜.\mathcal{D}[\rho]=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle A_{j},[\rho]_{{\omega_{j}}}^{-1}A_{j}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\ .

Now replace ρ\rho by ρ⁡(t):=𝒫t†​ρ\rho(t):={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho and let us assume that ρ\rho is in the domain of ℒ†{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}, a trivial assumption in the finite dimensional case. Then

dd​t​ρ​(t)=𝒫t†​(ℒ†​ρ)=𝒫t†​(div⁡(𝐀)),\frac{\rm d}{{\rm d}t}\rho(t)={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}\rho)={\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}({\rm div}({\bf A}))\ ,

and assuming that 𝒫→t\vec{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} defined by (8.12) intertwines with 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}, we have that

𝐀⁡(t)=e−λ​t​(𝒫t†​A1,…,𝒫t†​A|𝒥|).{\bf A}(t)=e^{-\lambda t}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{1},\dots,{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{|{\mathcal{J}}|})\ .

Therefore, by the convexity argument used in the proof of Theorem 8.3

𝒟⁡[𝒫t†​ρ]=e−2​λ​t​∑j∈𝒥⟨𝒫t†​Aj,[𝒫t†​ρ]ωj−1​𝒫t†​Aj⟩ℌ𝒜≤e−2​λ​t​𝒟​[ρ].\mathcal{D}[{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho]=e^{-2\lambda t}\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{J}}}\langle{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{j},[{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho]_{{\omega_{j}}}^{-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}A_{j}\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}}}\leq e^{-2\lambda t}\mathcal{D}[\rho]\ .

By a standard argument, the generalized log-Sobolev inequality (8.17) follows immediately for ρ\rho in the domain of ℒ†{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}^{\dagger}. In summary, if one is interested more in entropy dissipation inequalities than the geodesic convexity of the entropy Theorem 5.10 together with an intertwining relation allows one to bypass the Riemannian structure. This fact also underlines the utility of writing the evolution equation as gradient flow for the entropy, which is essential for the argument.

In the rest of this section we explain how intertwining formulas may be proved. We consider two examples, already introduced, namely the Bose and Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroups. In the Fermi case, we are within the scope of the finite dimensional picture developed here, and we will be able to prove the geodesic convexity of the relative entropy. In the Bose case, we are in an infinite dimensional setting, and work remains to be done to rigorously prove the geodesic convexity in this case. However, by what has been explained in the preceding paragraphs, we shall obtain a rigorously valid generalized logarithmic Sobolev inequality.

8.2. Intertwining via commutation formulas

For both the Fermi and Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroups 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}, there is a Mehler type formula for 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} from which the intertwining can be readily checked. In the Fermi case, this can be found in formulas (4.1) and (4.2) of [11], and the formula in the Bose case is a simple adaptation of this.

Fortunately however, it is not necessary to find an explicit formula for the action of the semigroup 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} to prove the intertwining identity and (8.12). In case where such identities are true, they can often be readily checked using the form of the generator ℒ{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}.

8.4 LEMMA.

Let 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} be the Bose Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup with generator ℒβ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta} given in (6.17), and let σβ\sigma_{\beta} be its invariant state. Then for all ρ∈𝔖+\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+},

8.6 THEOREM.

For β≥0\beta\geq 0, let 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} be the Fermi Ornstein-Uhlenbeck semigroup with generator ℒβ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta} given in (6.8), and let σβ\sigma_{\beta} be its invariant state. Then for all ρ∈𝔖+\rho\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+},

D(𝒫tρ||σβ)≤e−2​λβ​tD(ρ||σβ)D({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}\rho||\sigma_{\beta})\leq e^{-2\lambda_{\beta}t}D(\rho||\sigma_{\beta})

where λβ=min{cosh(βej/2):j=1,…,m}\lambda_{\beta}=\min\{\cosh(\beta e_{j}/2)\ :\ j=1,\dots,m\}. Moreover, the realtive entropy functional ρ↦D(ρ||σβ)\rho\mapsto D(\rho||\sigma_{\beta}) is geodesically λβ\lambda_{\beta} convex in the Riemannain metric associated to ℒβ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{\beta}.

8.3. Talagrand type inequalities

Our final results in this section extend a result from outr earlier paper [12] to the present more generla setting. The proof is step-for-step the one from our previous paper, with only minor modifications, and we shall thereofre be brief. However, it is worth recording the more general result since this subject has recently attracted the attention of other researchers [43, 63].

The connection between logarithmic Sobolev inequalities and transport inequalities of Talagrand type [69] was originally discovered and developed by Otto and Villani [56]. The fact that a Talgrand type inequlaity holds for our transport metric is further evidence that it is indeed a bona-fide transport metric.

8.7 THEOREM (Talagrand type inequality).

Let ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} be the generator of an ergodic QMS that satisifes the σ\sigma-DBC with respect to σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}. Suppose that the generalized logarithmic Sobolev inequality (8.17) is valid for some λ>0\lambda>0. (8.19) d⁡(ρ,σ)≤2D(ρ||σ)λ.d(\rho,\sigma)\leq\sqrt{\frac{2D(\rho||\sigma)}{\lambda}}\ .

Since the evolution described by t↦𝒫t†​ρt\mapsto{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}^{\dagger}\rho is gradient flow for the relative entropy, gρ⁡(t)(ρ˙(t),ρ˙(t))=−ddtD(ρ(t)||σ){\displaystyle g_{\rho(t)}(\dot{\rho}(t),\dot{\rho}(t))=-\frac{{\rm d}}{{\rm dt}}D(\rho(t)||\sigma)} so that for any 0≤t1<t2<∞0\leq t_{1}<t_{2}<\infty,

(8.20) ∫t1t2gρ⁡(t)​(ρ˙​(t),ρ˙​(t))​𝑑t≤t2−t1​D(ρ(t1)||σ)−D(ρ(t2)||σ).\int_{t_{1}}^{t_{2}}\sqrt{g_{\rho(t)}(\dot{\rho}(t),\dot{\rho}(t))}\>{\rm d}t\leq\sqrt{t_{2}-t_{1}}\sqrt{D(\rho(t_{1})||\sigma)-D(\rho(t_{2})||\sigma)}\ .

Fix any ϵ>0\epsilon>0. Define the sequence of times {tk}\{t_{k}\}, k∈ℕk\in{\mathord{\mathbb{N}}},

tk−tk−1≤ϵ2​λ.t_{k}-t_{k-1}\leq\frac{\epsilon}{2\lambda}\ .

Then by (8.20), with this choice of {tk}\{t_{k}\},

∫tk−1tkgρ⁡(t)​ρ​(t)​(ρ˙​(t),ρ˙​(t))​𝑑t\displaystyle\int_{t_{k-1}}^{t_{k}}\sqrt{g_{\rho(t)}{\rho(t)}(\dot{\rho}(t),\dot{\rho}(t))}\>{\rm d}t ≤ϵ2​λ(e−(k−1)​ϵ−e−k​ϵ)D(ρ||σ)\displaystyle\ \leq\ \sqrt{\frac{\epsilon}{2\lambda}(e^{-(k-1)\epsilon}-e^{-k\epsilon}){D(\rho||\sigma)}}
=D(ρ||σ)2​λe−kϵ/2ϵ⁡(eϵ−1).\displaystyle\ =\ \sqrt{\frac{D(\rho||\sigma)}{2\lambda}}e^{-k\epsilon/2}\sqrt{\epsilon(e^{\epsilon}-1)}\ .

Appendix A Proof of Theorem 3.1

In this appendix we present a simple and self-contained proof of Theorem 3.1. The starting point is an isometry that is crucial to the characterization of quantum Markov semigroup generators given by Gorini, Kossakowski and Sudarshan [31]:

For any finite dimensional Hilbert space ℌ{\mathfrak{H}}, let 𝒞2​(ℌ){\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}) denote the linear operators from ℌ{\mathfrak{H}} to ℌ{\mathfrak{H}} equipped with the normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product ⟨A,B⟩𝒞2​(ℌ)=(dim⁡(ℋ))−1​Tr​[A∗​B]\langle A,B\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}})}=({\rm dim}(\mathcal{H}))^{-1}{\rm Tr}[A^{*}B] so that ‖𝟏‖ℌ=1\|{{\bf 1}}\|_{{\mathfrak{H}}}=1. As above, we use †\dagger for the Hermitian adjoint in 𝒞2​(ℌ){\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}). A special case deserves a special notation: let ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} denote the n×nn\times n complex matrices ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) equipped with this same normalized Hilbert-Schmidt inner product.

A particular orthonormal basis in ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} plays a distinguished role in what follows: For 1≤i,j≤n1\leq i,j\leq n, let Ei,jE_{i,j} denote the n×nn\times n matrix whose i,ji,j entry is 11, and whose other entries are all 00. If {e1,…,en}\{e_{1},\dots,e_{n}\} is the standard basis of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, then Ei,jE_{i,j} is the rank one operator that is written as |ei⟩​⟨ej||e_{i}\rangle\langle e_{j}| in a standard quantum mechanical notation introduced before. In this notation, one has

(A.1) Ei,j⊗Ei,j=(|ei⟩​⟨ej|)⊗(|ei⟩​⟨ej|)=|ei⊗ei⟩​⟨ej⊗ej|.E_{i,j}\otimes E_{i,j}=(|e_{i}\rangle\langle e_{j}|)\otimes(|e_{i}\rangle\langle e_{j}|)=|e_{i}\otimes e_{i}\rangle\langle e_{j}\otimes e_{j}|\ .

It follows that

(A.2) 1n​∑i,j=1nEi,j⊗Ei,j=|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|whereΨ=1n​∑j=1nej⊗ej\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}E_{i,j}\otimes E_{i,j}=|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|\quad{\rm where}\quad\Psi=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{j=1}^{n}e_{j}\otimes e_{j}

is a rank one projection in ℂn⊗ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\otimes{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, and, in particular, is positive. This observation is due to Choi, and some of the simple but fundamental conclusions he drew from it are related below. More immediately, {Ei,j}1≤i,j≤n\{E_{i,j}\}_{1\leq i,j\leq n} is an orthonormal basis of ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} called the matrix unit basis.

There is a natural identification of 𝒞2​(ℌn){\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n}) with ℌn⊗ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}\otimes{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} that takes advantage of the multiplication on ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}: For A,B∈ℌnA,B\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}, define the operator #⁡(A⊗B):ℌn→ℌn\#(A\otimes B):{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}\to{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} by

#⁡(A⊗B):ℳn​(ℂ)→ℳn​(ℂ),#⁡(A⊗B)​X=A​X​B,\#(A\otimes B):\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})\to\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})\ ,\qquad\#(A\otimes B)X=AXB\ ,

for all X∈ℌnX\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}. It follows that the adjoint of #⁡(A⊗B)\#(A\otimes B) as an operator on ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} is given by (#⁡(A⊗B))†=#⁡(A∗⊗B∗)\big(\#(A\otimes B)\big)^{\dagger}=\#(A^{*}\otimes B^{*}). Moreover,

(A.3) Tr⁡[#⁡(A⊗B)]=Tr⁡[A]​Tr​[B].\displaystyle{\rm Tr}[\#(A\otimes B)]={\rm Tr}[A]{\rm Tr}[B]\ .

The left-hand side of (A.3) involves the trace for operators on ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}, whereas the right-hand side involves the trace for operators on ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}.

A.1 LEMMA.

Let {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\} and {Gβ}\{G_{\beta}\} be two orthonormal bases of ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}, so that {Fα⊗Gβ}\{F_{\alpha}\otimes G_{\beta}\} is an orthonormal basis of ℌn⊗ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}\otimes{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}. Then {#⁡(Fα⊗Gβ)}\{\#(F_{\alpha}\otimes G_{\beta})\} is orthonormal in 𝒞2​(ℌn){\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n}). In particular, the map #\# is unitary from ℌn⊗ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}\otimes{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} into 𝒞2​(ℌn){\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n}).

Proof of Lemma A.1.

We may compute the trace on ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} using any orthonormal basis, and using the matrix unit orthonormal basis {Ei,j}1≤i,j≤n\{E_{i,j}\}_{1\leq i,j\leq n}, we have for all α,β\alpha,\beta and μ,ν\mu,\nu,

⟨#⁡(Fα⊗Gβ),#⁡(Fμ⊗Gν)⟩𝒞2​(ℳn​(ℂ))\displaystyle\langle\#(F_{\alpha}\otimes G_{\beta}),\#(F_{\mu}\otimes G_{\nu})\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}(\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}))} =\displaystyle= n−2​∑i,j=1nTr⁡[(Fα​Ei,j​Gβ)∗​Fμ​Ei,j​Gν]\displaystyle n^{-2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}{\rm Tr}[(F_{\alpha}E_{i,j}G_{\beta})^{*}F_{\mu}E_{i,j}G_{\nu}]
=n−2​∑i,j=1nTr⁡[Gβ∗​Ej,i​Fα∗​Fμ​Ei,j​Gν]\displaystyle=n^{-2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}{\rm Tr}[G_{\beta}^{*}E_{j,i}F_{\alpha}^{*}F_{\mu}E_{i,j}G_{\nu}] =\displaystyle= n−2​∑i,j=1n(Gν​Gβ∗)j,j​(Fα∗​Fμ)i,i\displaystyle n^{-2}\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}(G_{\nu}G_{\beta}^{*})_{j,j}(F_{\alpha}^{*}F_{\mu})_{i,i}
=\displaystyle= n−1​Tr​[Gν​Gβ∗]​n−1​Tr​[Fα∗​Fμ]=δα,μ​δβ,ν.\displaystyle n^{-1}{\rm Tr}[G_{\nu}G_{\beta}^{*}]n^{-1}{\rm Tr}[F_{\alpha}^{*}F_{\mu}]=\delta_{\alpha,\mu}\delta_{\beta,\nu}\ .

∎

Consider any linear transformation 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), and hence on ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}. Let {Fβ}\{F_{\beta}\} be any orthonormal basis of ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}. Then {Fα∗}\{F_{\alpha}^{*}\} is also an orthonormal basis of ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}, and by Lemma A.1, {#⁡(Fα∗⊗Fβ)}\{\#(F_{\alpha}^{*}\otimes F_{\beta})\} is an orthonormal basis of 𝒞2​(ℌn){\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n}). Thus 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} has the expansion

(A.4) 𝒦=∑α,βcα,β​#​(Fα∗⊗Fβ).{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}\#(F_{\alpha}^{*}\otimes F_{\beta})\ .

or, what is the same,

(A.5) 𝒦​(A)=∑α,βcα,β​Fα∗​A​Fβfor​all​A∈ℳn​(ℂ),{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}\qquad{\rm for\ all}\ A\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})\ ,

where the coefficients cα,βc_{\alpha,\beta} are given by

(A.6) cα,β=⟨#⁡(Fα∗⊗Fβ),𝒦⟩𝒞2​(ℌn).c_{\alpha,\beta}=\langle\#(F_{\alpha}^{*}\otimes F_{\beta}),{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})}\ .

This orthonormal expansion is fundamental to the work of Gorini, Kossakowski and Sudarshan on the structure of generators of quantum Markov semigroups.

A.2 DEFINITION.

The n2×n2n^{2}\times n^{2} matrix cα,βc_{\alpha,\beta} with entries given by (A.6) is called the GKS matrix for the operator 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} with respect to the orthonormal basis {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\}. When we wish to emphasize the dependence on 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}, we write cα,β​(𝒦)c_{\alpha,\beta}({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}).

A.3 Remark.

Let A,B∈ℳn​(ℂ)A,B\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) and consider the case 𝒦=#⁡(A⊗B){\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}=\#(A\otimes B). By the isometry proved in Lemma A.1, the GKS matrix of 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is given by

cα,β\displaystyle c_{\alpha,\beta} =⟨#⁡(Fα∗⊗Fβ),#⁡(A⊗B)⟩𝒞2​(ℌn)=⟨Fα∗⊗Fβ,A⊗B⟩ℌn⊗ℌn\displaystyle=\langle\#(F_{\alpha}^{*}\otimes F_{\beta}),\#(A\otimes B)\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})}=\langle F_{\alpha}^{*}\otimes F_{\beta},A\otimes B\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}\otimes{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}}
=n−2​Tr​[Fα​A]​Tr​[Fβ∗​B].\displaystyle=n^{-2}{\rm Tr}[F_{\alpha}A]{\rm Tr}[F^{*}_{\beta}B]\ .

In particular, the identity transformation on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) results from the choice A=B=𝟏A=B={{\bf 1}}, and so the GKS matrix of the identity transformation is the rank-one matrix

(A.7) cα,β=n−2​Tr​[Fα]​Tr​[Fβ∗].c_{\alpha,\beta}=n^{-2}{\rm Tr}[F_{\alpha}]{\rm Tr}[F^{*}_{\beta}]\ .

This formula will be useful later on.

The following lemma is from [31]; for the convenience of the reader we give a short proof.

A.4 LEMMA.

Let 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} be a linear operator on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), and let {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\} be an orthonormal basis of ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). Then the GKS matrix of 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} with respect to {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\} is self-adjoint if and only if (𝒦​A)∗=𝒦​A∗({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A^{*} for all A∈ℳn​(ℂ)A\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}).

Proof.

Write 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} as in (A.4) and define 𝒦~​(A):=(𝒦​A∗)∗\widetilde{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A):=({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A^{*})^{*}. Then

𝒦~​(A)=(∑α,βcα,β​Fα∗​A∗​Fβ)∗=∑α,βcα,β¯​Fβ∗​A​Fα=∑α,βcβ,α¯​Fα∗​A​Fβ.\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A)=\Big(\sum_{\alpha,\beta}c_{\alpha,\beta}F_{\alpha}^{*}A^{*}F_{\beta}\Big)^{*}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\overline{c_{\alpha,\beta}}F_{\beta}^{*}AF_{\alpha}=\sum_{\alpha,\beta}\overline{c_{\beta,\alpha}}F_{\alpha}^{*}AF_{\beta}\ .

By the uniqueness of the expansion (A.4), 𝒦~=𝒦\tilde{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} if and only if cα,β=cβ,α¯c_{\alpha,\beta}=\overline{c_{\beta,\alpha}} for all α,β\alpha,\beta. ∎

The GKS matrix of a linear transformation 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} from ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) to ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) is closely related to the Choi matrix of 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}. Let {Ei,j}1≤i,j≤n\{E_{i,j}\}_{1\leq i,j\leq n} be matrix unit basis of ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}. The Choi matrix of 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is the element of ℳn2​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n^{2}}({\mathbb{C}})

(A.8) C⁡(𝒦)=∑i,j=1n𝒦​(Ei,j)⊗Ei,j,C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})=\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})\otimes E_{i,j}\ ,

viewed as the n×nn\times n block matrix with entries in ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) whose i,ji,j entry is 𝒦​(Ei,j){\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j}).

If we now identify ℂn⊗ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\otimes{\mathbb{C}}^{n} with ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) by identifying v⊗wv\otimes w with ∑i,j=1nvi​wj​Ei,j\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}v_{i}w_{j}E_{i,j}, C⁡(𝒦)C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}) becomes an operator on ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}.

The identity provided by the following lemma was pointed out in [58], and used there to simplify part of the proof [31] of their theorem on the structure of generators of quantum Markov semigroups on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}).

A.5 LEMMA.

Let 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} be a linear operator on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), and let C⁡(𝒦)C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}) be defined by (A.8). Identify ℂn⊗ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\otimes{\mathbb{C}}^{n} with ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) by identifying v⊗wv\otimes w with ∑i,j=1nvi​wj​Ei,j\sum_{i,j=1}^{n}v_{i}w_{j}E_{i,j}, so that C⁡(𝒦)C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}) is identified with an operator on ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}. Then for all F,G∈ℌnF,G\in{\mathfrak{H}}_{n},

(A.9) ⟨G,C⁡(𝒦)​F⟩ℌn=⟨#⁡(G⊗F∗),𝒦⟩𝒞2​(ℌn)\langle G,C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})F\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}}=\langle\#(G\otimes F^{*}),{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})}
Proof.

By direct computation,

⟨G,C⁡(𝒦)​F⟩ℌn\displaystyle\langle G,C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})F\rangle_{{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}} =\displaystyle= ∑k,ℓ,m,p=1nG¯k,m​[𝒦​(Ei,j)]k,ℓ​[Ei,j]m,p​Fℓ,p\displaystyle\sum_{k,\ell,m,p=1}^{n}\overline{G}_{k,m}[{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})]_{k,\ell}[E_{i,j}]_{m,p}F_{\ell,p}
=\displaystyle= ∑k,ℓ,m,p=1nFℓ,p​[Ej,i]p,m​G¯k,m​[𝒦​(Ei,j)]k,ℓ\displaystyle\sum_{k,\ell,m,p=1}^{n}F_{\ell,p}[E_{j,i}]_{p,m}\overline{G}_{k,m}[{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})]_{k,\ell}
=\displaystyle= ∑k,ℓ=1n(F​Ej,i​G∗)ℓ,k​[𝒦​(Ei,j)]k,ℓ\displaystyle\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}(FE_{j,i}G^{*})_{\ell,k}[{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})]_{k,\ell}
=\displaystyle= ∑k,ℓ=1n(G​Ei,j​F∗)ℓ,k∗​[𝒦​(Ei,j)]k,ℓ=⟨#⁡(G⊗F∗),𝒦⟩𝒞2​(ℌn).\displaystyle\sum_{k,\ell=1}^{n}(GE_{i,j}F^{*})^{*}_{\ell,k}[{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(E_{i,j})]_{k,\ell}=\langle\#(G\otimes F^{*}),{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\rangle_{{\mathcal{C}}_{2}({\mathfrak{H}}_{n})}\ .

∎

A fundamental theorem of Choi [15] says that a linear transformation 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) is completely positive if and only if its Choi matrix C⁡(𝒦)C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}) is positive as an operator on ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}. Indeed, in the notation of (A.2)

C⁡(𝒦)=n​𝒦⊗𝟏ℳn​(ℂ)​(|Ψ⟩​⟨Ψ|),C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})=n{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\otimes{{\bf 1}}_{\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})}\left(|\Psi\rangle\langle\Psi|\right)\ ,

Hence, when 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is completely positive, C⁡(𝒦)C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}) is positive. The converse is also true: Choi used an elementary spectral decomposition [15] to show that when C⁡(𝒦)C({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}) is positive, then 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is completely positive.

A.6 Remark.

The identity (A.9) shows that if {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\} is any orthonormal basis of ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n}, then the GKS matrix of 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} with respect to this basis is positive if and only if 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is completely positive. In other words, the GKS representation (A.5) of a linear operator 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) is well-suited to the question of whether 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is completely positive or not.

Going forward, it will be convenient to assume that our orthonormal bases {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\} of ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} are indexed by α∈{1,…,n}×{1,…,n}\alpha\in\{1,\dots,n\}\times\{1,\dots,n\}, and we write α=(α1,α2)\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}). For such bases, we make the following definition:

A.7 DEFINITION.

Let ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} be an operator on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) such that ℒ​𝟏=0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=0 and (ℒ​A)∗=ℒ​A∗({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}A^{*} for all A∈ℳnA\in\mathcal{M}_{n}. Let {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\} be any orthonormal basis of ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} such that F(1,1)=𝟏F_{(1,1)}={{\bf 1}}. Let cα,βc_{\alpha,\beta} be the GKS matrix for ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} with respect to {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\}. The (n2−1)×(n2−1)(n^{2}-1)\times(n^{2}-1) matrix with entries cα,βc_{\alpha,\beta} where α\alpha and β\beta range over the set {(i,j): 1≤i,j≤nand(i,j)≠(1,1)}\{(i,j)\ :\ 1\leq i,j\leq n\quad{\rm and}\quad(i,j)\neq(1,1)\} is called the reduced GKS matrix of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} for the basis {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\}.

The following lemma is due to Parravinci and Zecca [58]:

A.8 LEMMA.

Let ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} be a linear operator on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), and let 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}. Let {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\} be an orthonormal basis for ℌn{\mathfrak{H}}_{n} with F(1,1)=𝟏F_{(1,1)}={{\bf 1}}. Let cα,βc_{\alpha,\beta} be the GKS matrix of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} with respect to {Fα}\{F_{\alpha}\}. Then 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is completely positive for all t≥0t\geq 0 if and only if the reduced GKS matrix of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is positive.

Proof.

Suppose that 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is completely positive for each t>0t>0. By (A.7), the GKS matrix of the identity transformation is

(A.10) cα,β​(I)=δα,(1,1)​δβ,(1,1).c_{\alpha,\beta}(I)=\delta_{\alpha,(1,1)}\delta_{\beta,(1,1)}\ .

In particular, the reduced GKS matrix of the identity is zero. Then since

cα,β​(t−1​(𝒫t−I))=t−1​cα,β​(𝒫t)−t−1​cα,β​(I),c_{\alpha,\beta}(t^{-1}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}-I))=t^{-1}c_{\alpha,\beta}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t})-t^{-1}c_{\alpha,\beta}(I)\ ,

it follows that the reduced GKS matrix of t−1​(𝒫t−I)t^{-1}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}-I) coincides with the reduced GKS matrix of t−1​𝒫tt^{-1}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}, and by Remark A.6 this is positive. Taking the limit t→0t\to 0, we conclude that the reduced GKS matrix of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is positive.

Conversely, suppose that the reduced GKS matrix of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is positive. For small t>0t>0,

cα,β​(𝒫t)=cα,β​(I)+t​cα,β​(ℒ)+o⁡(t)c_{\alpha,\beta}({\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t})=c_{\alpha,\beta}(I)+tc_{\alpha,\beta}({\mathord{\mathscr{L}}})+o(t)

By (A.10), this is positive for all sufficiently small tt. By Remark A.6, 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is completely positive for all sufficiently small t>0t>0. Then by the semigroup property, 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is completely positive for all t>0t>0. ∎

For the converse, if ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} has the specified form, one restores the cjc_{j}’s by normalizing the VjV_{j}’s, and then writes ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} in its GKS form for this orthonormal basis (after including 𝟏{{\bf 1}} and any VjV_{j}’s with cj=0c_{j}=0). The reduced GKS matrix of ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is unchanged as the argument starting from (A.13) shows. Thus, by Remark A.6, ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} generates a completely positive semigroup 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}, and evidently ℒ​𝟏=0{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=0, so that 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is a QMS. The σ\sigma-DBC is then readily checked (using the fact that the VjV_{j} are eigenvectors of Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}). ∎

A.12 Remark.

It is easy to check the existence of an extension of 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} from 𝒜{\mathord{\mathscr{A}}} to ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) in many relevant cases; e.g., when 𝒜{\mathord{\mathscr{A}}} is a Clifford algebra with an odd number of generators. One might hope that there is a general extension using the conditional expectation.

Recall that for any unital C∗C^{*}-subalgebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} of ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), there is the conditional expectation E𝒜E_{\mathcal{A}} which is the orthogonal projection in ℌℳn​(ℂ){\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})} onto ℌ𝒜{\mathfrak{H}}_{\mathcal{A}} [72]. This may be written as an average over the unitaries in the commutant of 𝒜\mathcal{A} [10, 71]; the connected component of this group 𝔘\mathfrak{U} that contains the identity is a Lie subgroup of S​U​(n)SU(n), on which there exists a normalized Haar measure μ\mu, and then for all X∈ℳn​(ℂ)X\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), E𝒜​X=∫𝔘U∗​X​U​𝑑μ​(U){\displaystyle E_{\mathcal{A}}X=\int_{\mathfrak{U}}U^{*}XU{\rm d}\mu}(U). Evidently, E𝒜E_{\mathcal{A}} is a completely positive map with E𝒜​𝟏=𝟏E_{\mathcal{A}}{{\bf 1}}={{\bf 1}}. That is, E𝒜E_{\mathcal{A}} is a quantum Markov operator.

If 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is a linear transformation on 𝒜\mathcal{A}, define a linear transformation 𝒦^\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) by 𝒦^=𝒦∘E𝒜\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}\circ E_{\mathcal{A}}. Note that when a linear operator 𝒫{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}} on 𝒜\mathcal{A} is completely positive, so is 𝒫^\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}, and the restriction of 𝒫^\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}} to 𝒜\mathcal{A} is simply 𝒫{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}. Moreover, if ℒ1{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{1} and ℒ2{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{2} are two linear transformations of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, then ℒ^2​ℒ^1=ℒ2​ℒ1^\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{2}\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{1}=\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{2}{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}_{1}}. In this way we can “lift” any QMS 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} on 𝒜\mathcal{A} up to a one-parameter family of Markov operators 𝒫^t\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) such that for all s,t≥0s,t\geq 0, 𝒫t^​𝒫s^=𝒫t+s^\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}}\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{s}}=\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t+s}}. This construction fails to yield a semigroup only because limt→0𝒫^t=E𝒜\lim_{t\to 0}\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=E_{\mathcal{A}} and not limt→0𝒫^t=I𝒜\lim_{t\to 0}\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=I_{\mathcal{A}}. However, if 𝒫t=et​ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=e^{t{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}, then limt→01t​(𝒫^t−E𝒜)=ℒ^{\displaystyle\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t}(\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}-E_{\mathcal{A}})=\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}}. The operator ℒ^\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is evidently a self-adjointness preserving linear transformation from ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) to ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}), and ℒ^​𝟏=0\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}{{\bf 1}}=0. If 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} satisfies the σ\sigma-DBC for σ∈𝔖+​(𝒜)\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}(\mathcal{A}), then for all A,B∈ℳn​(ℂ)A,B\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}),

τ⁡[σ​B∗​𝒫^t​A]=τ⁡[σ​B∗​E𝒜​𝒫t​(E𝒜​A)]=τ⁡[(E𝒜​(B​σ)∗)​𝒫t​(E𝒜​A)]=τ⁡[σ​(E𝒜​B)∗​𝒫t​(E𝒜​A)],\tau[\sigma B^{*}\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}A]=\tau[\sigma B^{*}E_{\mathcal{A}}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(E_{\mathcal{A}}A)]=\tau[(E_{\mathcal{A}}(B\sigma)^{*}){\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(E_{\mathcal{A}}A)]=\tau[\sigma(E_{\mathcal{A}}B)^{*}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}(E_{\mathcal{A}}A)]\ ,

where we have used the fact that since σ∈𝒜\sigma\in\mathcal{A}, E𝒜​(σ​B∗)=σ​E𝒜​B∗E_{\mathcal{A}}(\sigma B^{*})=\sigma E_{\mathcal{A}}B^{*}. It follows that for each t≥0t\geq 0, 𝒫^t\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is self-adjoint with respect to the σ\sigma-GNS inner product on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). Consequently, the same is true of ℒ^\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}.

Therefore, the proof of Theorem 3.1 given just above shows that ℒ^\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} has the form specified in Theorem 3.1 except that some cjc_{j}’s might be negative: Applicability of Lemma A.8 requires that limt→0𝒫t=Iℳn​(ℂ)\lim_{t\to 0}{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=I_{\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}})}.

Appendix B Note on KMS-symmetry

We give a construction of a class of operators 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} that satisfy (𝒦​A)∗=𝒦​A∗({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A)^{*}={\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A^{*} for all AA and that are self-adjoint with respect to the σ\sigma-KMS inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩1/2\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2} for some σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}, but which do not commute with Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}, and consequently are not self-adjoint with respect to the σ\sigma-GNS inner product. An operator 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) that is self-adjoint with respect to ⟨⋅,⋅⟩1/2\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2} for some σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} is called KMS-symmetric.

When 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is completely positive with 𝒦​(𝟏)=𝟏{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}({{\bf 1}})={{\bf 1}}, it has a Kraus representation

𝒦​(A)=∑j=1mKj∗​A​Kjwhere∑j=1mKj∗​Kj=𝟏{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}(A)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}K_{j}^{*}AK_{j}\quad{\rm where}\quad\sum_{j=1}^{m}K^{*}_{j}K_{j}={{\bf 1}}\

for some set {K1,…,Km}⊂ℳn​(ℂ)\{K_{1},\dots,K_{m}\}\subset\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). Evidently, 𝒦†​A=∑j=1mKj​A​Kj∗{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}A=\sum_{j=1}^{m}K_{j}AK_{j}^{*}. Suppose that 𝒦†​σ=σ{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}\sigma=\sigma with σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+}. The dual set of Kraus operators {K^1,…,K^m}\{\widehat{K}_{1},\dots,\widehat{K}_{m}\} is given by

K^j=Δ1/2σKj∗=σ1/2Kj∗σ−1/2.\widehat{K}_{j}=\Delta^{1/2}_{\sigma}K_{j}^{*}=\sigma^{1/2}K_{j}^{*}\sigma^{-1/2}\ .

Then ∑j=1mK^j∗​K^j=𝟏{\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{m}\widehat{K}^{*}_{j}\widehat{K}_{j}={{\bf 1}}} and ∑j=1mK^j​σ​K^j∗=σ\displaystyle{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\widehat{K}_{j}\sigma\widehat{K}_{j}^{*}=\sigma}. It follows that the operator 𝒦^\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} defined by 𝒦^​A=∑j=1mK^j∗​A​K^j{\displaystyle\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A=\sum_{j=1}^{m}\widehat{K}^{*}_{j}A\widehat{K}_{j}} is completely positive with 𝒦^​(𝟏)=𝟏\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}({{\bf 1}})={{\bf 1}} and 𝒦^​†​(σ)=σ{{\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}}}}\,\mbox{}^{\dagger}(\sigma)=\sigma. A simple calculation shows that ⟨𝒦^​B,A⟩1/2=⟨B,𝒦​A⟩1/2\langle\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}B,A\rangle_{1/2}=\langle B,{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A\rangle_{1/2} for all A,B∈ℳn​(ℂ)A,B\in\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}). Thus, 𝒦^\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is the adjoint of 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} with respect to the σ\sigma-KMS inner product, and 𝒦^​𝒦\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is a completely positive operator on ℳn​(ℂ)\mathcal{M}_{n}({\mathbb{C}}) such that 𝒦^​𝒦​(𝟏)=𝟏\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}({{\bf 1}})={{\bf 1}} and (𝒦^​𝒦)†​σ=σ(\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})^{\dagger}\sigma=\sigma.

Define a quantum Markov semigroup 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} by

𝒫t=∑n=0∞e−t​tnn!​(𝒦^​𝒦)n=et⁡(𝒦^​𝒦−I).{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}e^{-t}\frac{t^{n}}{n!}(\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})^{n}=e^{t(\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}-I)}\ .

Evidently 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} is KMS-symmetric for each t>0t>0 since 𝒦^​𝒦\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is KMS-symmetric. Furthermore, 𝒫t{\mathord{\mathscr{P}}}_{t} commutes with Δσ\Delta_{\sigma} for each t>0t>0 if and only if 𝒦^​𝒦\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} commutes with Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}. We will show that the latter is not generally the case.

To construct counterexamples, consider n=2n=2; the construction that follows is readily generalized. Let {u1,u2}\{u_{1},u_{2}\} be an orthonormal basis in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} and let {v1,v2}\{v_{1},v_{2}\} be a set of two linearly independent unit vectors in ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2} that are not orthogonal. Define the rank-one operators K1K_{1} and K2K_{2} by Kj=|vj⟩​⟨uj|K_{j}=|v_{j}\rangle\langle u_{j}|, j=1,2j=1,2. Evidently, K1∗​K1+K2∗​K2=𝟏K_{1}^{*}K_{1}+K_{2}^{*}K_{2}={{\bf 1}}, and we define 𝒦​A=K1∗​A​K1+K2∗​A​K2{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}A=K_{1}^{*}AK_{1}+K_{2}^{*}AK_{2} so that 𝒦​𝟏=𝟏{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{{\bf 1}}={{\bf 1}}. Then the range of 𝒦†{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger} is spanned by {|v1⟩​⟨v1|,|v2⟩​⟨v2|}\big\{|v_{1}\rangle\langle v_{1}|\ ,\,|v_{2}\rangle\langle v_{2}|\big\}. A simple computation yields

where

with a=|⟨v1,u2⟩|2a=|\langle v_{1},u_{2}\rangle|^{2} and b=|⟨v2,u1⟩|2b=|\langle v_{2},u_{1}\rangle|^{2}, and since {v1,v2}\{v_{1},v_{2}\} is not orthogonal, a+b>0a+b>0. The vector (ba)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}b\\ a\end{array}\right) is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 11, and hence

satisfies 𝒦†​σ=σ{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger}\sigma=\sigma, and hence, as we just noted, (𝒦^​𝒦)†​σ=σ(\widehat{{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}})^{\dagger}\sigma=\sigma. The other eigenvalue of the matrix in (B.1) is 1−a−b<11-a-b<1, so that (B.2) gives the unique invariant state. It follows that the eigenvalues of 𝒦†{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger} are 11, 1−a−b1-a-b and 00, with

Null⁡(𝒦†)=Span⁡{|u1⟩​⟨u2|,|u2⟩​⟨u1|}.{\rm Null}({\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}^{\dagger})={\rm Span}\big\{|u_{1}\rangle\langle u_{2}|\ ,\ |u_{2}\rangle\langle u_{1}|\big\}\ .

Consequently, the null space of 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is 22-dimensional as well, and same holds for the null space of 𝒦^​𝒦\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}, since 𝒦^\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} is the σ\sigma-KMS dual of 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}. By ergodicity, it is the only eigenspace of 𝒦^​𝒦\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}} with this property.

Generically, σ\sigma will have two distinct eigenvalues. (For example, take {u1,u2}\{u_{1},u_{2}\} to be the standard basis of ℂ2{\mathbb{C}}^{2}, and take v1=12​(11)v_{1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ 1\end{array}\right) and v2=15​(12)v_{2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ 2\end{array}\right), so that σ=17​[2335]\sigma=\frac{1}{7}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}2&3\\ 3&5\end{array}\right].) Under this condition, the first equality in (B.3) would yield ⟨η1,v1⟩=0\langle\eta_{1},v_{1}\rangle=0. Thus, with this choice of 𝒦{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}, ℒ:=𝒦^​𝒦−I{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}}:=\widehat{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}{\mathord{\mathscr{K}}}-I is the generator of a quantum Markov semigroup with invariant state σ∈𝔖+\sigma\in{\mathfrak{S}}_{+} such that ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is self-adjoint with respect to the σ\sigma-KMS inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩1/2\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{1/2}, but such that ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} does not commute with Δσ\Delta_{\sigma}. It follows that ℒ{\mathord{\mathscr{L}}} is not self-adjoint with respect to the GNS inner product.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
